detail.abstract: The rapid deployment of AI systems in regulated domains has outpaced the governance mechanisms needed to constrain them at runtime. This paper introduces the Computable Trust Architecture (CTA), a framework for runtime AI governance that treats trust as a computable, attributable, temporally valid, and policy-enforceable property of AI-mediated actions and outputs. As a reference implementation of CTA, the Trust Computation System (TCS) computes a Trust Integrity Score (TIS) over governed dimensions under a resolved policy configuration parameterized by risk tier, action class, and connection context, and produces a Trust Certificate (TC) as a tamper-evident, hash-chained, identity-attributed governance artifact suitable for audit and regulatory examination. We present the formal mathematical basis of the framework, its architectural components, a reference implementation passing 108 specification unit tests, controlled evaluations across financial services and healthcare governance scenarios, and a model of trust dynamics covering loss, drift, and recovery. The framework addresses a structural gap in contemporary AI governance between policies that specify intended behavior and enforcement mechanisms capable of governing action at runtime.

title: PETs in Context: An Exploration of Privacy-enhancing Technologies for Everyday Internet use
affiliations: Technical University of Munich, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and University of Cologne

detail.title: PETs in Context: An Exploration of Privacy-enhancing Technologies for Everyday Internet use
detail.abstract: Social interactions are increasingly mediated by the internet, which results in severe privacy threats for internet users. One way to respond to such threats is the use of privacy-enhancing technologies (PETs), whose purpose it is to allow for better management of information flows in social computing systems like the internet. However, PETs are often designed from a technical perspective and, apart from usability concerns, poorly aligned with the privacy threats perceived by users in different contexts. This study addresses privacy management on the internet from a user-centered perspective to derive implications for PET design. We explore how internet-savvy users report to use PETs in everyday internet contexts with a qualitative research approach. The findings showcase how internet-savvy users select and use PETs and are consolidated in a process model. Finally, we synthesize three important design considerations: privacy harm-oriented PET selection, context-sensitive PET use, and informative PET evaluations.

detail.abstract: Efficient and reliable disaster monitoring from social media posts is crucial for early detection of at-risk individuals requiring evacuation or seeking humanitarian assistance; however, existing image-only approaches, such as DisasterNet, overlook the socio-technical requirements of transparency, contextual reasoning, and computational efficiency necessary for real-world deployment in crisis settings. To address these challenges, we introduce DissaMM, a novel lightweight multimodal neural architecture for disasterrelated post classification. Methodologically, DissaMM integrates frozen ResNet-50 and BERT encoders to extract complementary image-text features, fused through a compact multi-layer perceptron for efficient classification. Post-hoc explainability is incorporated via LIME and SHAP, enabling transparent attribution over both visual regions and textual tokens. Empirically, DissaMM achieves substantial gains over unimodal and computationally heavier baselines-such as CNN-based, ViT-based, and state-space models-across five classification tasks (Time-Period, Urgency, Relevancy, Damage, Relief). Notably, it improves Damage (F1-macro ↑ 0.6973 → 0.8500) and Relief (F1-micro ↑ 0.7568 → 0.9343), while maintaining extreme efficiency (1.51M trainable parameters, 3.02 GFLOPs, >35k images/sec inference, <700 MB memory). In addition, evaluation on the MS-COCO Captions benchmark shows that DissaMM generalizes beyond the crisis domain, achieving captioning performance comparable to strong transformer baselines. Beyond performance, ablation studies further confirm the stability and interpretability advantages of structured multimodal fusion over unimodal alternatives. Altogether, this work advances a socio-technical perspective on explainable AI in crisis informatics, demonstrating how design choices in model architecture can operationalize human-centered explainability-balancing robustness, transparency, and efficiency to support real-time disaster monitoring from social media posts, with the potential to enhance situational awareness and aid rapid response efforts.

title: Computational Framework for Measuring Strategic Opportunities Based on Structural Hole Theory
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), University of British Columbia (UBC) - Sauder School of Business, University of British Columbia (UBC) - Sauder School of Business and UBC Sauder School of Business

detail.title: Computational Framework for Measuring Strategic Opportunities Based on Structural Hole Theory
detail.abstract: Although opportunities are central to firm innovation and performance, prior research lacks a scalable, theory-grounded approach to measuring them. Existing measures are either context-specific or detached from explicit relational mechanisms, limiting their generalizability and interpretability. Leveraging computational methods including text analytics, unsupervised machine learning, and network analysis of large-scale digitized data, we propose a computational design framework guided by structural hole theory that enables fine-grained strategic opportunity measures: hole-opening, hole-entering, and non-hole positions. We validate this framework through systematic analysis of IPO outcomes using U.S. public firm panel data. The results show that hole-opening positions are associated with higher post-IPO valuations, but with a lower likelihood of M&A exits, whereas hole-entering and non-hole positions are linked to lower IPO valuations but higher probabilities of M&A outcomes. These patterns reveal distinct opportunity roles based on firms’ relative structural positions. This computational framework contributes to IS research by offering a replicable, theory-driven foundation for opportunity measurement.

detail.abstract: The 44 questions and answers in this Gemini discussion led to some promising discoveries about how AI might someday be able to replicate human language experiences using 3-Dimensional Narrative Mapping. The formulae for Question #34 were stress tested in Claude AI and corrections were found which lends credibility to the proposed methods. This article is nearly 19,000 words in length, but the entire discussion must be read so that the reader follows the logic leading to the discoveries-and possibilities! Current models for predicting adolescent behavioral outcomes frequently suffer from the "absolute flaw of the mean," aggregating disparate socio-emotional data points into a statistical average that erases individual variance and cultural "vividness." This paper introduces a human-centric, tri-axial framework designed to map individual experience as a specific geometric coordinate within an eight-octant "semantic landscape." Drawing upon the Logos as a fundamental architectural unit of reality, the model utilizes three primary dimensions for mapping: (1) Linguistic Deficit (Ld), measuring the gap between a subject's traumatic experience and their internal vocabulary for processing; (2) Social Valence (Sv), quantifying peer-group exclusion or inclusion weight; and (3) Tolerance Buffer (Tb), modeled as a dynamic integer representing internal resilience. Through a series of case studies-ranging from adolescent peer rejection to acute moral injury-we demonstrate how Monte Carlo (MC) simulations, integrated with literary archetypal datasets (e.g., Hawthorne, Dickens, O'Connor), can identify "Coordinates of Crisis" before behavioral "burn-in" occurs. We argue that AI's primary utility lies not in autonomous agency, but as a "diagnostic tether" capable of identifying linguistic poverty in a subject's environment. The findings suggest that by shifting the predictive focus from the "standard person" to the "Standard Deviation of the Soul," we can intervene with highresolution accuracy to restore agency and meaning-capital to vulnerable individuals.

title: IT FEELS LIKE MINE: HOW PROMO CODES FOSTER PSYCHOLOGICAL OWNERSHIP AND TRANSFER IT TO ADVERTISED PRODUCTS

detail.abstract: Promo codes are ubiquitous in digital marketing, yet their psychological effects extend far beyond price reduction. Across four experimental studies (N = 631), this research demonstrates that promo codes function as psychological ownership vehicles-unique alphanumeric codes foster feelings that the discount is "mine," and these ownership feelings transfer from the discount to the advertised product itself. Study 1 (N = 99) establishes that advertisements containing promo codes with uniqueness cues significantly increase psychological ownership of the discount (M = 4.36 vs. 3.49, p = .031), which fully mediates effects on willingness to redeem, share, explore, and perceived value. Study 2 (N = 100) disentangles code format effects, revealing that unique random-character codes elevate ownership significantly more than generic codes or no codes (mean difference = 1.06, p = .038), even without any explicit uniqueness messaging. Study 3 (N = 218) enriches the promotional context with text-based personalization and uniqueness descriptions, showing that promo codes significantly heighten perceived personalization (eta-sq = .17), uniqueness (eta-sq = .16), and psychological ownership (eta-sq = .13). Parallel mediation analysis reveals that among personalization, uniqueness, and ownership, psychological ownership is the only significant individual mediator of purchase likelihood (indirect = 0.24, 95% CI [0.005, 0.51]). Study 4 (N = 214) introduces the critical transfer-of-ownership mechanism: serial mediation analysis confirms that promo code presence increases discount ownership, which increases product ownership, which increases purchase intention (serial indirect = 0.18, 95% CI [0.07, 0.29]). Personal traits-need for control, endowment sensitivity, and materialism-consistently moderate the promo code-to-ownership pathway. These findings reframe promo codes from transactional tools to psychological ownership instruments that create product attachment before purchase occurs.

title: From Discs to Downloads: New Legal Risks of Software Distribution and Licensing under EU Law

detail.title: From Discs to Downloads: New Legal Risks of Software Distribution and Licensing under EU Law
detail.abstract: This essay discusses how the shift of software distribution from discs to platform-based downloads and cloud services has transformed the legal risks of distributing software and licensing it under EU law. It provides an overview of the fundamental legal framework, especially the Software Directive, the Consumer Rights Directive, the Digital Content Directive, the Digital Services Act, the Digital Markets Act, and the new Product Liability Directive. Based on the ruling by the CJEU in UsedSoft v Oracle and later academic literature on digital exhaustion, it finds three major issues: the unclear distinction between ownership and access, unfair and limiting licensing in digital platform ecosystems, and the complicated division of liability among faulty or insecure software. The essay holds that, despite recent EU efforts that modernise some areas of the regime, there still exist gaps that erode the rights of users and legal certainty. It suggests specific changes to define when software transactions are to be considered as sales to enhance the control over unfair platform licensing and enforce a balanced liability regime on software to protect the users and maintain the incentive to innovate.

title: The Intention Gap: A Behavioural Framework for Sunscreen Non-Adoption in Families

detail.title: The Intention Gap: A Behavioural Framework for Sunscreen Non-Adoption in Families
detail.abstract: Despite widespread awareness of UV harm, daily sunscreen adoption in families remains low. This paper proposes the Intention Gap as the structural mechanism responsible: defined as the space between a person's awareness of UV harm and their daily act of applying sunscreen. The gap is not caused by ignorance. It is caused by two proposed behavioural variables : Sunscreen Resistance, the accumulated friction a person carries toward sunscreen application, and Consequence Salience, how vivid and personally real the future harm of UV exposure feels at the moment of decision. The Intention Gap is directly proportional to Sunscreen Resistance and inversely proportional to Consequence Salience. Closing the gap requires two targeted interventions in sequence: first, reducing resistance through a first best product impression; second, raising salience through targeted education delivered to the primary family health decision maker. The framework has implications for product design, brand communication, and public health intervention strategy.

title: The Ontological Challenge Artificial Intelligence Poses To Criminal Law

detail.title: The Ontological Challenge Artificial Intelligence Poses To Criminal Law
detail.abstract: Every previous technological revolution left a human at the end of the causal chain: a publisher, an owner, a driver. Artificial intelligence breaks this fundamental structure. AI systems produce outputs that mimic human agency yet originate in statistical processes involving no mind. This paper argues that criminal law's core doctrines cannot be effectively applied to AI-generated harms. Mens rea fails because there is no mind to examine, and actus reus fails because there is no act to attribute. The deeper problem is ontological: AI is a non-agent that produces agentlike effects, falling outside the law's existing categories of person, tool, and natural force. Without a fix, courts will face a choice between accepting AI-caused harms as mere misfortune or scapegoating whichever human happened to be proximate when the system caused damage. This paper proposes that accountability must be built into the infrastructure surrounding AI before deployment, including device-level cryptographic authentication, chain-of-custody verification, and user-set autonomy limits, developed primarily by the private market and standardized by government. These tools do not resolve the ontological gap, but they restore a traceable record of human choice that criminal law can meaningfully assess.

title: Algorithmic Subversion of Consumer Sovereignty: A Computational and Ethical Analysis of AI-Induced Impulse Buying in the Indian Digital Economy

detail.title: Algorithmic Subversion of Consumer Sovereignty: A Computational and Ethical Analysis of AI-Induced Impulse Buying in the Indian Digital Economy
detail.abstract: The Challenge of Hyper-Nudging The rapidly evolving landscape of the Indian digital retail sector presents an exigent challenge to foundational concepts of consumer autonomy and market rationality. This study critically examines the rise of AI-driven choice architecture-a socio-technical system where proprietary machine learning models transcend mere predictive analytics to become agents of demand manufacturing and endogenous impulse generation. With the Indian ecommerce valuation trajectory soaring past $350 billion by 2030, the opaque, dynamic interplay between immutable human cognitive heuristics and relentless algorithmic optimization loops demands sophisticated, interdisciplinary scrutiny. This comprehensive thesis executes a rigorous mixed-methods investigation into the precise influence of advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) nudges-specifically hyper-personalized recommendation manifolds, programmed psychological scarcity mechanisms, and real-time dynamic pricing protocols-on the volume and velocity of impulse purchasing across major Indian digital platforms (Amazon, Flipkart, Zomato, Zepto, Nykaa). Drawing philosophically from Thaler's Nudge Theory, grounding its cognitive analysis in Kahneman's Dual System Theory, and extending its scope to the cutting-edge domain of Hyper-Nudging, this work establishes a quantifiable link between complex machine learning architecture and inherent consumer psychological vulnerabilities. The methodological framework combines a large-scale quantitative survey (N=200), a controlled laboratory experiment (N=60) utilizing a bespoke "ShopSim" environment, and granular technical deconstruction of platform-specific algorithms. The empirical findings underscore a critical phenomenon: algorithmic social proof generates demonstrable conformity effects, while personalized recommendation engines strategically bypass high-effort, deliberative "System 2" processing, funnelling users into high-velocity transaction pathways. Crucially, the research details a measurable geographical divergence in algorithmic response, wherein consumers in emerging Tier 2/3 markets exhibit a higher Trust Paradox-uncritically accepting algorithmic suggestions as authoritative-than their Tier 1 counterparts. The analysis concludes with a trenchant critique of the reactive Consumer Protection Act (2019) and proposes prescriptive, actionable policy provisions for the Digital India Act, advocating for mandatory Algorithmic Accountability and the statutory establishment of Consumer Sovereignty by Design.

detail.abstract: Since digital technology is more expensive and ever-changing, it is transforming the potential and practicality of marketing. Nowadays, companies have become more agile, data-driven, and ROI focused. The outbreak of the novel SARS-CoV-2, along with advances in machine learning and artificial intelligence, represents a tremendous breakthrough for the era of digital marketing. The ultimate goal of machine learning and artificial intelligence (ML/AI) is to deliver data and insights to brands so they can figure out what is working and what is not. This will help marketers determine which types of communications are effective and how to distribute them. As a result, numerous marketing companies apply these promising strategies. AI uses machine learning to adapt and make immediate changes that impact marketing. The exact impact of events like the COVID-19 pandemic is difficult to predict, but AI will help us track and anticipate them, as well as provide the data we need to move forward. This Paper discusses contemporary studies that have used advanced technology to increase the number of researchers, address problems and obstacles, and aid marketing specialists in addressing real-world concerns by employing such algorithms. AI-driven marketing uses models to automate, optimize, and augment the transformation of data into actions and interactions, anticipating needs, forecasting behaviors, and hyper-personalizing messaging. Modern marketers use modern data to create hyper-individualized and hyper-contextualized brand messages, with each message building on prior customer encounters. These interactions are considered as a way to choreograph future encounters in a satisfying virtuous loop, rather than as the end of a consumer journey. Managers must examine marketing demands for automation, optimization, and augmentation in relation to the sought-after benefits of prediction, anticipation, and personalization when developing an AI strategy. Managers must proactively analyze their company to reorganize roles and responsibilities, and to clearly define the division of activities between humans and computers, balancing machine-inspired goals with projected benefits.

title: Remote Work and AI Use: Evidence from a Worker Panel

detail.title: Remote Work and AI Use: Evidence from a Worker Panel
detail.abstract: Does remote work drive AI adoption? Using longitudinal worker data, I document that fully remote and hybrid workers are 6.8 and 6.1 percentage points more likely to report frequent AI use than otherwise similar, remote-feasible onsite workers. Both differences collapse to near zero once identification exploits within-person changes in remote status. Event-study estimates show no pre-trends and no post-transition shifts, and the within-worker null holds even in the most AI-exposed, remote-capable occupations. The remote-work premium in AI use reflects sorting on worker type and task content, not a causal effect of the arrangement.

detail.abstract:
The healthcare industry operates within an increasingly dynamic and competitive environment, influenced by rapid technological innovation, evolving patient expectations, and stringent regulatory frameworks. This study titled “Evaluating the Competitive Landscape and Identifying Key Success Factors in the Healthcare Industry” explores the major drivers that determine the competitive position of healthcare organisations. The primary objectives are to analyse the existing competitive forces shaping the healthcare sector, identify the factors that contribute to sustainable success, and provide strategic recommendations for improving performance. A mixed-method research approach was employed, integrating secondary data from published industry reports with primary insights from healthcare professionals through surveys and interviews. Analytical frameworks such as Porter’s Five Forces, PESTEL, and VRIO were used to assess both external and internal determinants of competitiveness. Findings revealed that digital transformation, regulatory compliance, patient experience, cost efficiency, and strategic partnerships are the most critical success factors influencing long-term viability.

The research concludes that healthcare organisations must prioritise digital capability enhancement, regulatory readiness, and data-driven decision-making to strengthen their market positioning. Strategic collaboration with technology partners and continuous innovation were found to be essential for maintaining a sustainable competitive edge.

title: Visibility ≠ Credibility: Self-Promotion Bias in LLM-Generated Recommendations

detail.title: Visibility ≠ Credibility: Self-Promotion Bias in LLM-Generated Recommendations

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and Perplexity AI are increasingly used as recommendation engines for professional services including marketing consultants and digital agencies. This paper investigates a structural bias in LLM recommendation outputs: the tendency to surface self-promoted brands as apparently credible due to co-occurrence patterns in retrieval data. Through direct query testing across four major LLM platforms and systematic source analysis-including a direct on-record acknowledgement by ChatGPT of its own bias-this research establishes that visibility in AI-generated recommendations does not equate to independently validated credibility. The paper identifies three primary self-promotion patterns, proposes a five-point buyer verification framework, and examines implications for the practice of Generative Engine Optimization (GEO). Findings suggest that until LLMs develop robust mechanisms for distinguishing self-referential authority signals from independently verified credibility, buyers should apply structured verification when using AI for professional service recommendations.

detail.abstract:
AI-generated answers are changing how prospective students discover and evaluate universities because systems interpret queries, select sources, and construct responses before a user visits a website. This shifts visibility from ranking position alone to observable behaviour within generated outputs, where inclusion, attribution, and recommendation determine which institutions are considered.

This paper presents an applied framework for evaluating university AI search visibility using four outcome layers: AI search inclusion, AI brand mentions, AI recommendation behaviour, and AI referral traffic. The study applies this framework to a controlled dataset of Computer Science queries executed across multiple AI systems, including ChatGPT, Google AI Overview, Perplexity, Claude, Gemini, and Grok.

The results show that visibility is concentrated among a limited set of universities, with repeated inclusion and recommendation driven by content structure, entity clarity, and external reinforcement rather than traditional ranking position alone. Institutions that provide structured, topic-aligned content and maintain consistent representation across external sources are more likely to be selected and recommended within generated answers.

The findings demonstrate that university visibility is increasingly determined at the point of answer construction. This requires a shift from ranking-focused optimisation to content and entity strategies aligned with how AI systems interpret, synthesise, and present information during student discovery.

detail.abstract: This study investigates how live sports streaming via virtual reality (VR) and mobile applications, enabled by advanced B5G/6 G networks, shapes the viewing experience and influences users' willingness to adopt immersive streaming technologies. The pilot described in this paper took place during a professional basketball game in Madrid, Spain, and tested two immersive streaming scenarios: a VR-based experience and a mobilebased experience. Both scenarios relied on low-latency, high-bandwidth, high-throughput network capabilities and delivered 360 • live video content. Participants evaluated the quality and impact of their immersive viewing experience. Data collected from both groups was analyzed using partial least squares multi-group analysis to assess perceived ease of use, usefulness, enjoyment, and flow experience. The results show that B5G/6G-enabled immersive live streaming significantly enhances all measured aspects of user perception across both scenarios. Although the strength of specific relationships varied slightly between the VR and mobile groups, no statistically significant differences emerged. Overall, the findings confirm that next-generation networks can effectively support high-quality immersive experiences and offer valuable guidance for the future deployment of real-time entertainment technologies across different platforms.

declarations.ethicsApproval: All survey participants provided informed consent prior to participation. No personally identifiable information was collected. Interview participants consented to the use of anonymized quotations from their responses.

detail.abstract:
This thesis explores the role of ethics, morality, and sustainability in shaping consumer decision-making within the fashion and beauty industries. It investigates the tension between what consumers say they believe and what they actually do, uncovering the drivers behind the value-action gap that continues to challenge ethical and sustainable retail efforts. By combining quantitative survey data with demographic segmentation and qualitative analysis, this study provides an in-depth look at how consumer behavior is influenced not just by values, but by access, privilege, and social context.

The research demonstrates that factors such as income, education, geography, etc., play a significant role in determining how consumers perceive ethicality and sustainability - and more importantly, whether they feel empowered to act on those beliefs. While consumers with higher socioeconomic status were more likely to report alignment with ethical values, this appeared more a reflection of flexibility and convenience than deeper morality. Conversely, lower-income consumers often shared similar ideals but lacked the financial or logistical means to act in line with them, highlighting the systemic nature of ethical consumption.

The thesis introduces the Strategic Sustainability Integration Model (SSIM), a practical framework designed to help brands embed ethical principles into their business without placing the burden of responsibility solely on the consumer. The model accounts for factors such as brand transparency, ease of access, pricing strategy, and cultural alignment - showing how businesses can strategically lower the barriers to sustainable purchasing.

This research challenges the traditional narrative that ethical consumption is simply a matter of individual choice. Instead, it reframes it as a complex interaction between moral intention, structural limitations, and commercial design. The findings offer practical recommendations for luxury, fast fashion, and beauty brands - particularly in the MENA region - seeking to create more inclusive and sustainable consumer pathways. By understanding and addressing the real reasons why consumers fall short of their values, brands can design better systems, build stronger loyalty, and drive more meaningful changes in the industry.

title: The Income Effect in Advertising: Evidence from Housing Cost Shifts

detail.title: The Income Effect in Advertising: Evidence from Housing Cost Shifts
detail.abstract: Income is a fundamental determinant of consumer demand, yet we lack causal evidence on how income affects advertising responsiveness. We address this gap by exploiting housing cost shocks as an exogenous income shifter, instrumenting local housing price growth in a shift-share IV design, and estimating how income conditions moderate TV advertising effectiveness for 78 restaurant brands across 13 million store-weeks. We find that a one standard deviation increase in local housing cost growth nearly eliminates the baseline advertising elasticity for restaurants, with the IV estimate roughly eight times larger than the naive observational estimate. This negative housing cost-interaction effect is amplified in areas with higher renter shares, consistent with housing cost pressure operating as a negative income shock through rent increases, and effects are also significantly larger for high ad-spend brands, which show greater incomedriven variance in ad effectiveness. Applying our estimates to observed housing cost trends, our projections imply that advertising elasticities swing by 0.15 or more as income conditions change, suggesting that optimal ad allocation levels may vary substantially with economic conditions. Smaller-sample evidence from 22 supermarket brands recovers a significant positive effect of income (housing cost) shocks on grocery store ad elasticity, indicating that the direction of the effect is category-specific.

title: The Effects of Hope-based Interventions on Vaccine Adoption: Outcomes From Two Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Trials
affiliations: University of Rhode Island and University of Rhode Island

detail.title: The Effects of Hope-based Interventions on Vaccine Adoption: Outcomes From Two Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Trials

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors report no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: All studies were approved by the Institutional Review Board at the University of Rhode Island.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the National Science Foundation (award # 2027620).

detail.abstract: Hope as an emotion is integral to consumption contexts, as marketers sell hope through their value propositions. Despite its importance, marketing research paid little attention to the emotionspecific motivational influence of hope. The current research utilized two longitudinal randomized controlled trials in explicating the effects of hope-based interventions on consumers' vaccination decisions. Both the studies were conducted during the initial phase of the COVID-19 vaccine rollout. The first study was a 4-week longitudinal randomized controlled trial that studied the effects of hope-based interventions through in-depth educational materials. The second study was an 8-week randomized controlled trial where the effects of nudge-based interventions of hope were examined. Both the studies revealed strong negative effects of hope-based interventions (vs. benchmark vs. situational control) on vaccine hesitancy. We predict and find that panic induced anxiety during the pandemic enhances vaccine hesitancy, and hope-framed interventions is effective in reducing vaccine hesitancy through mitigating the effects of panic. Our findings offer critical advancements to the Hope Theory and the Protection Motivation Theory. Theoretical and practical implications are discussed.

title: Sovereign Risk with Endogenous Debt Limits
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago and Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago

detail.title: Sovereign Risk with Endogenous Debt Limits

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Chicago Working Paper No. 2026-08
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Why do countries set sovereign debt ceilings if they keep raising them? This paper shows that debt ceilings can serve as intermediate commitment devices that reduce expected dilution, thereby lowering spreads—and their volatility—even without reducing total borrowing. We propose a new sovereign default model with long-term debt in which each government inherits a previously announced ceiling but may revise it by paying a political or institutional deviation cost. This friction generates a state-dependent form of partial commitment. The ceiling mitigates debt dilution at the expense of fiscal flexibility, leading the government to voluntarily adopt a ceiling that limits the discretion of its future selves. Governments choose rules that are costly—but not impossible—to adjust, trading off lower spreads and volatility through reduced dilution against the option value of fiscal flexibility in bad times. Consistent with this mechanism, we show that emerging-market countries operating under fiscal rules exhibit lower sovereign spreads and lower spread volatility, even though breaches and revisions occur.

title: Climate Transition Risks and Bank Lending: Evidence from Colombia
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Geneva Graduate Institute and Geneva Graduate Institute

detail.title: Climate Transition Risks and Bank Lending: Evidence from Colombia
detail.abstract: This paper examines how the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement affected bank lending to fossil-fuel firms in Colombia, an emerging fossil-fuel-dependent economy. Using confidential loan-level data from the Colombian credit registry covering the period 2010–2019, we implement a difference-in-differences framework to compare credit volumes and loan pricing for fossil-fuel firms relative to firms in other sectors following the Agreement. We find that Colombian banks reduced credit to fossil-fuel firms by approximately 46% in the post-Paris period, with no corresponding new increases in interest rates. Banks also became more selective, reallocating toward larger and better-capitalized fossil fuel firms. The contraction in credit supply is particularly pronounced among banks with high pre-existing fossil-fuel lending (“brown banks”), which reduced overall lending more aggressively and increased interest rates by an average of 2.15 percentage points across borrowers. These findings raise important concerns for financial stability in emerging economies with high dependence on fossil fuels.

title: Tokenized Stock Markets: Tracking Quality, Arbitrage Limits, and Price Discovery
affiliations: University of Missouri at Saint Louis and University of Missouri at Saint Louis

detail.title: Tokenized Stock Markets: Tracking Quality, Arbitrage Limits, and Price Discovery
detail.abstract: ​We provide a systematic empirical assessment of tokenized equity secondary markets, studying 57 Backed Finance xStock tokens from June 2025 through April 2026. We identify and correct a date-labeling offset in the RWA.xyz data: without the one-day UTC correction, token–stock return correlations have a median of 0.063; after correction the median is 0.656, a prerequisite for valid inference. The pooled tracking slope is β̂ = 0.871 (R² = 0.514), below near-perfect NAV tracking; token age and underlying volatility explain 57% of cross-sectional variation. Price-to-NAV deviations revert at a half-life of 0.4 trading days. Despite continuous blockchain operation, token returns over exchange-closed intervals yield β̂ ≈ 0 across 1,959 non-trading events (R² ≤ 0.005): the infrastructure for off-hours price discovery is in place but market depth is insufficient to realize it. These results provide the benchmark against which the NYSE and Nasdaq tokenization initiatives can be measured as they scale.

title: Foundations and Knowledge Clusters in TikTok (Douyin) Research: Evidence From Bibliometric and Topic Modelling Analyses
affiliations: Széchenyi István University, Kautz Gyula Faculty of Economics, Department of Logistics and Forwarding, Students, Higher Institute of Computer Science of El Manar, University of Rome Tor Vergata and MODUL University Vienna

detail.title: Foundations and Knowledge Clusters in TikTok (Douyin) Research: Evidence From Bibliometric and Topic Modelling Analyses

publicationDetails.detailsText: Multimedia Tools and Applications, volume 83, issue 11, 2024[10.1007/s11042-023-16768-x]

detail.abstract: The goal of this study is to comprehensively analyze the dynamics and structure of TikTok research since its initial development. The scholarly composition of articles dealing with TikTok was dissected via a bibliometric study based on a corpus of 542 journal articles from the Scopus database. The results show that TikTok research has flourished in recent years and also demonstrate that the authors' collaboration networks are disjointed, indicating a lack of cooperation among TikTok researchers. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that research collaboration among academic institutions reflects the North-South divide, also highlighting a limited research collaboration between institutions in developed and developing countries. Based on the keyword co-occurrence network and topic modeling, Tik-Tok research revolves mainly around five thematic areas, including public health, health communication and education, platform governance, body image, and its impact on children and students. Based on these findings, numerous suggestions for further research are offered. As far as the authors are aware, this is the first application of bibliometrics and topic modeling to assess the growth of TikTok research and reveal the intellectual base of this knowledge domain.

title: Interest Rate Sensitivity and Valuation Dynamics of NBFCs: Evidence from India with Cross-Market Insights

detail.title: Interest Rate Sensitivity and Valuation Dynamics of NBFCs: Evidence from India with Cross-Market Insights
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how interest rate cycles influence the financial performance and market valuation of Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) in emerging markets. While traditional financial theory suggests that rising interest rates compress margins and pressure valuations, this research explores why certain retail lenders demonstrate remarkable resilience. Utilizing a quantitative case study design, the paper analyzes Shriram Finance (India) and Capitec Bank (South Africa) over the complete rate cycle of FY2021-2025. The study tracks five key metrics, including Net Interest Margins (NIM) and Price-to-Book (P/B) multiples. The findings reveal that Shriram Finance achieved a significant 222bps NIM expansion and a sustained P/B re-rating despite aggressive rate hikes, driven by structural liability lags and high customer segment captivity. In contrast, Capitec experienced more traditional valuation compression. These results challenge conventional rate-sensitivity assumptions, suggesting that liability management and borrower captivity are more dominant determinants of valuation resilience than the magnitude of the rate shock itself.

title: Algorithmic Trading and Information Dynamics Around Unscheduled Corporate Events
affiliations: University of Mississippi, University of Mississippi and University of Mississippi

detail.title: Algorithmic Trading and Information Dynamics Around Unscheduled Corporate Events
detail.abstract: Prior work establishes that algorithmic trading (AT) deters information acquisition around scheduled events, but whether this extends to unscheduled corporate events is unknown. Using a sample of unexpected special dividend announcements, we find that abnormal AT activity (measured as deviations from firm-specific baselines) widens pre-announcement informational gaps. To measure the informational asymmetries, we develop a standardized price jump measure which allows us to preserve over 50% of observations that would be discarded using prior price jump approaches. Our findings indicate that aggregate AT activity declines for approximately 20 trading days following special dividend announcements, persisting longer than that observed around regular dividend benchmarks. This withdrawal pattern suggests that AT strategies profit from information asymmetry rather than information processing; when information asymmetries are publicly resolved, AT activity appears to decline.

title: Beyond Membership: The Institutional Embeddedness of Trade Unions and Their Persistence in Financialised European Banking

detail.title: Beyond Membership: The Institutional Embeddedness of Trade Unions and Their Persistence in Financialised European Banking

keywords: and Labour Costs P16 -Political Economy of Capitalist System

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the persistence of trade unions in European banking despite sustained declines in membership density, falling labour-capital ratios, and increasing financialisation of the sector. While existing research consistently documents long-term decline in the unionisation rate across advanced economies, it offers limited understanding of how unions continue to exert influence in highly financialised and technologically transformed industries such as banking, where traditional foundations of collective organisation have been significantly weakened. Addressing this gap, the paper develops an institutionalist framework that shifts analytical attention from membership density to institutional embeddedness within governance and bargaining structures. It argues that union influence in European banking is not primarily determined by membership base but by the degree of structural integration into sectoral bargaining systems, organisational routines, and procedural rights integrated in restructuring processes. Within this configuration, unions operate as intermediary actors that buffer adjustment pressures, enable coordination, and shape the implementation of organisational change. The main hypothesis is that union persistence in European banking is explained primarily by institutional embeddedness rather than membership density, and that integrated unions function as stabilising actors within financialised organisational environments. An auxiliary hypothesis proposes that declining labour-capital ratios increase the functional relevance of unions by intensifying coordination challenges and raising demand for procedural mechanisms of restructuring and employment adjustment. Methodologically, the study adopts a multi-layered mixed-methods design combining quantitative sectoral indicators-union density, employment trends, banking assets, and labour-capital ratioswith qualitative evidence drawn from comparative analysis of collective bargaining systems, country case studies, semi-structured interviews, and survey data. This design enables a structured multi-level analysis linking macro-structural financialisation dynamics with meso-institutional arrangements and micro-organisational processes. The paper contributes to three strands of literature. First, it challenges density-centred accounts of union decline by demonstrating that organisational erosion does not necessarily imply institutional marginalisation. Second, it extends research on financialisation by showing how structural transformation in banking coexists with persistent forms of procedural labour inclusion. Third, it contributes to comparative political economy by conceptualising unions as embedded institutions that enhance coordination and systemic stability in financialised capitalism. Overall, the findings show that union power in European banking is not disappearing but being reconfigured through institutional integration within contemporary governance structures, producing a systematic decoupling between organisational size and institutional influence.

title: Trade Policy Uncertainty and the Macroeconomic Transmission of Rare Earth Prices
affiliations: University of Turin - Collegio Carlo Alberto, Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro, Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Trade Policy Uncertainty and the Macroeconomic Transmission of Rare Earth Prices
detail.abstract: Trade policy uncertainty transmits through strategic commodity markets to amplify macroeconomic shocks. This paper investigates the transmission of trade policy uncertainty (TPU) via rare-earth and critical-mineral prices using a Bayesian Structural Vector Autoregression model for the U.S. economy (1994Q1-2024Q4). Point estimates suggest TPU shocks induce persistent decreases in strategic material prices and transitory production increases followed by contraction, though wide 99% credible intervals indicate substantial uncertainty. Forecast error variance decompositions provide complementary evidence: TPU explains approximately 10% of the variance in strategic material prices and aggregate output, confirming its role as a non-trivial macroeconomic driver.

title: The Impact of the Circular Economy Transition on Green Jobs in Europe: a Panel VAR Analysis
affiliations: University of Turin - Collegio Carlo Alberto, Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro, Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Impact of the Circular Economy Transition on Green Jobs in Europe: a Panel VAR Analysis

declarations.funderStatement: Matteo Bondesan acknowledges financial support under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP), Mission 4, Component 2, Investment 1.1, Call for tender No. 1409 published on 14.9.2022 by the Italian Ministry of University and Research (MUR), funded by the European Union – NextGenerationEU– Project Title "Measuring, managing and hedging indirect climate-transition risks" – CUP P20228CHNL - Grant Assignment Decree No. 1376 adopted on 01/09/2023 by the Italian Ministry of Ministry of University and Research (MUR).

detail.abstract: The transition to a circular economy (CE) is a cornerstone of the European Green Deal, promising environmental sustainability and new avenues for employment. However, the empirical evidence on the link between circular economy practices and green job creation across the European Union remains limited. This study fills this gap by employing a Panel Vector Autoregressive (PVAR) model on data from Eurostat's Circular Economy Monitoring Framework (2005-2022) to analyse the dynamic relationships between key CE indicators and green employment. Our findings reveal that technological innovation, proxied by green patents, is the most potent and persistent driver of green job growth, accounting for a median of 35% of the forecast error variance. Improvements in waste management and recycling rates also generate positive employment effects, albeit with a more gradual and modest impact. The results underscore the systemic nature of the green transition, whereby interdependent and mutually reinforcing CE dimensions foster job creation.

title: Love of Enemy Assessment: Initial Evidence for Reliability and Validity
affiliations: , Harvard University - Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health, Harvard University, Harvard University, New College of Florida, Harvard University, Harvard University, Harvard University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Harvard University, Harvard University - Institute for Quantitative Social Science, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Harvard University and Baylor University

detail.title: Love of Enemy Assessment: Initial Evidence for Reliability and Validity

declarations.ethicsApproval: The Fordham University Institutional Review Board and Office of Regulatory Affairs and Research Compliance at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health granted approval for the studies. The studies were conducted in accordance with the local legislation and institutional requirements. The participants provided their written informed consent to participate in this study.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was also supported by the John Templeton Foundation grant 62731, “The Construct and Assessment of Interpersonal Love.”

detail.abstract: We introduce a new love of enemy assessment and report on evidence for its reliability and validity. The somewhat paradoxical notion of love of enemy concerns having a disposition to desire good for, and right relationships with, those who might be considered one's enemies; it in some sense constitutes a movement towards the ending of the enmity itself. We propose construct definitions for the notion of enemy, and also unitive (desiring right relationships with) and contributory (desiring good for) enemy love. We provide evidence for validity and reliability through item analysis, cognitive interviews (N=23), and quantitative analysis of two crosssectional samples (N=728 and N=10,290). Initial evidence from these studies supports reliability and validity, some distinction between unitive versus contributory enemy love, and distinctions with related notions of forgiveness. The love of enemy assessment helps provide a foundation for the empirical study of love of enemy, including its distribution, determinants, and effects, and how such love of enemy might be promoted to facilitate greater societal flourishing.

title: Firm Relocation Responses to Wildfire Events
affiliations: Oregon State University, Department of Applied Economics, Oregon State University and University of Idaho

detail.title: Firm Relocation Responses to Wildfire Events
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of wildfires on firm migration across the western United States using tract-level data from 2010 to 2019. We employ a quasi-experimental design that compares tracts that experienced a wildfire event to those that did not. The results show that wildfires lead to a measurable short-run increase in firm out-migration: in the first year after a wildfire, the number of firms exiting a tract rises by 11.4%. The effect diminishes in subsequent years, suggesting a short-term disruption rather than a persistent decline. These findings provide the first tract-level evidence that wildfires can trigger immediate business relocation responses. The estimated effects are driven entirely by non-rural counties and the service & retail sectors, where the increase in establishment relocation is both statistically and economically significant. In contrast, there is no detectable change in relocation behavior among establishments in rural counties. This is explained by our theoretical model, which predicts that the effect is driven by moving costs and a strong agglomeration economy, which makes it possible for firms in an urban county to relocate to nearby areas or other urban counties in the same metropolitan area and keep their access to workers, customers, suppliers, and business services.

detail.abstract: Este estudio analiza los principales determinantes de la diversificación productiva en el Perú, una economía caracterizada por una elevada concentración exportadora en recursos primarios y persistentes dificultades para transitar hacia actividades de mayor complejidad. Se propone una estrategia de triangulación para identificar restricciones estructurales e invariantes que condicionan la aparición de nuevos productos exportables. Los resultados convergen en tres hallazgos principales. Primero, la distancia en el espacio de productos constituye la principal barrera para la entrada de nuevas actividades. Segundo, la complejidad económica opera como un facilitador condicionado, efectivo únicamente cuando existe proximidad a capacidades productivas existentes. Tercero, los horizontes temporales de transformación productiva resultan considerablemente prolongados incluso bajo condiciones favorables. En conjunto, la evidencia revela una fuerte concentración de capacidades en sectores de baja competitividad, lo que limita las posibilidades de diversificación. Finalmente, el estudio identifica 50 productos oportunidad con probabilidades relativamente mayores de entrada, proporcionando una base empírica concreta para el diseño de políticas industriales selectivas orientadas a la diversificación productiva

title: Trustless Settlement for the Autonomous Economy: Sealed-Bid RFQ with HTLC Atomic Execution Across Heterogeneous Blockchains

detail.title: Trustless Settlement for the Autonomous Economy: Sealed-Bid RFQ with HTLC Atomic Execution Across Heterogeneous Blockchains
detail.abstract: We present Hashlock Markets, a protocol for cross-chain over-the-counter (OTC) settlement that eliminates counterparty risk by binding price discovery and asset exchange to a single hash-timelocked atomic execution. The crypto OTC market, estimated at hundreds of billions of US dollars in daily notional with no canonical reporting mechanism, currently relies on bilateral trust, custodial escrow, or centralized-exchange desks-each of which reintroduces the very counterparty exposure trustless settlement was meant to remove. The emergence of autonomous, large-language-model-driven agents as economic actors sharpens this problem: such agents own wallets, sign transactions, and transact at machine speed, but cannot complete custodial onboarding flows designed for human counterparties. Hashlock Markets addresses both populations through one settlement layer. A sealed-bid request-for-quote (RFQ) auction handles price discovery; a Hash Time-Locked Contract (HTLC) atomic swap, with matched timelocks across heterogeneous chains, handles execution. The protocol exposes the same interface to web users, programmatic clients, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) agents, supporting human-human, human-agent, and agentagent trades under identical guarantees. Five composed primitives-native-Bitcoin collateral vaults via header-oracle bridging, forward OTC delivery on a collateralized timelock, a tiered counterparty directory, multi-leg trade atomicity via shared-preimage chaining, and execution rewards coupled to KYC tier-are introduced and analyzed. To our knowledge, this is the first deployed implementation that combines crosschain HTLC atomic settlement with an MCP-native agent interface and reference settlements on Ethereum and Sui mainnet. Index Terms-hash time-locked contracts, atomic swap, cross-chain settlement, counterparty risk, request for quote, sealed-bid auction, model context protocol, autonomous agents, over-the-counter trading

detail.abstract: The accounting architecture for digital assets has developed unevenly. Under both IFRS and U.S. GAAP, recent technical activity has concentrated mainly on the holder-side of crypto-assets, while issuer-side token transactions remain fragmented across analogies to financial instruments, revenue contracts, loyalty programmes, provisions, and, in practice, non-recognition. That fragmentation is no longer tenable. Web3 issuers, centralised platforms, fintechs and traditional enterprises are now using tokens not only as fundraising devices, but also as access rights, governance mechanisms, customer-retention instruments, and promotional distribution tools. This paper develops a principles-based issuer-side model that separates token arrangements according to their economic substance rather than their technological form. The proposed framework proceeds through five decision gates: • (i) whether the token creates a contractual claim or residual interest within IAS 32 / IFRS 9; • (ii) whether it embodies an enforceable promise to transfer goods, services or network access within IFRS 15; • (iii) whether it grants a material right in a loyalty or rewards structure; • (iv) whether a promotional airdrop creates a substantive stand-ready obligation; and • (v) whether the token is, in substance, a governance-only digital right with no continuing issuer obligation. The paper argues that minting alone is ordinarily not a recognition event, that internally generated treasury tokens are not issuer assets, that governance tokens are not equity absent the IAS 32 residual-interest test, and that utility and loyalty tokens ordinarily create contract liabilities rather than immediate revenue. It also proposes a more disciplined treatment for promotional airdrops, together with journal-entry mechanics, disclosure requirements, market illustrations and a bridge to CPC and U.S. GAAP practice. The objective is to provide an auditable, globally usable foundation for the accounting of token issuance by issuers rather than holders.

title: The Strength of Weak Ties in Commons Governance: Militarized Enforcement, Elite Coalitions, and Cross-Community Coordination

detail.title: The Strength of Weak Ties in Commons Governance: Militarized Enforcement, Elite Coalitions, and Cross-Community Coordination
detail.abstract: A rich literature on common-pool resources demonstrates that strong intra-community ties-the dense bonds of kinship, friendship, and frequent interaction-underpin effective local governance by fostering trust, reciprocity, and robust monitoring. This understanding has spawned a dominant policy paradigm of "community fortification." However, many critical CPRs, such as fisheries, span multiple communities, creating an "inter-community domain" where the resource system is cross-boundary, while governance remains rooted in localized, intra-community dynamics. This disconnect explains why conventional community-based institutions often falter, as seen with East Africa's Beach Management Units (BMUs). Although legally mandated for inclusivity, BMUs remained anchored in localized structures and failed to enforce rules across communities, leaving cross-community overfishing unchecked. This article argues that governing these shared resources requires a different social architecture, where weak ties-Mark Granovetter's conceptualization of infrequent, instrumental bridges between social groupsbecome paramount. Analyzing the case of militarized fisheries governance on Buvuma Island, I identify a critical mechanism: while material capacity and policy-induced incentives created a constituency of compliant actors, a coalition of affluent fishermen was able to coordinate across communities by leveraging pre-existing, crosscommunity weak ties, formed through seasonal migration, to construct an inter-community network. This network strategically partnered with state enforcers, providing localized intelligence and financial resources essential for coordinated enforcement. This led to a sharp reduction in illicit fishing and a significant fish stock recovery, though at considerable social cost to poorer fishers excluded from the coalition. My findings reconceptualize the "strength of weak ties" within commons theory, illustrating that effective environmental governance beyond the local scale depends not only on resources or incentives, but on the social structures that enable their coordination across communities.

detail.abstract: This study analyzes the drivers of productive diversification in Peru using a triangulation approach to identify structural constraints shaping the emergence of new export activities. It finds that distance in the product space is the main barrier to diversification, while economic complexity supports entry only when countries are sufficiently close to existing capabilities. The results also highlight that structural transformation requires long time horizons, even under favorable conditions, and that Peru’s capabilities remain concentrated in low-competitiveness sectors, limiting diversification potential. Finally, the paper identifies 50 opportunity products with higher probabilities of entry, offering an empirical basis for designing targeted industrial policies.

title: Fictitious Play in Markov Potential Games

detail.title: Fictitious Play in Markov Potential Games
detail.abstract: We consider a variant of fictitious play dynamics that combines regularized Q-learning with smoothed fictitious play and analyze its convergence properties in Markov potential games. In the considered dynamics, players form a belief on the opponent strategies and based on such belief they form an estimate of their own continuation payoff (Q-function), then they take a smoothed best response using such payoff estimates. Under the key property that players update their beliefs about opponent strategies at a slower timescale compared to their estimates of their continuation payoffs, we show that the fictitious play dynamics converge to a set of approximate Nash equilibria in Markov potential games without model knowledge.

title: Fungibility, Not Quantity: A New Theory of Money and Inflation

detail.title: Fungibility, Not Quantity: A New Theory of Money and Inflation
detail.abstract: Does monetary expansion necessarily generate inflation? Standard monetary theory assumes that money is fully fungible across uses. This paper develops a framework of purpose-constrained currency (PoC), in which money is non-fungible and allocated to specific domains of expenditure, showing that the canonical relation MV=PYMV = PYMV=PY is incomplete under such a structure. When money is treated as a vector of domain-specific balances, inflation becomes a local rather than aggregate phenomenon, and monetary expansion can be inflation-neutral under conditions such as demand saturation and slack capacity. The analysis integrates general equilibrium, dynamic optimization, and mechanism design, and demonstrates robustness to partial fungibility, stochastic shocks, and heterogeneous agents, while also incorporating political economy constraints, labor mobility spillovers, and behavioral responses. It further shows that non-fungibility can be implemented through cryptographic enforcement, making the framework operational. Quantitative simulations indicate that targeted issuance can achieve near-zero inflation while improving welfare, suggesting that inflation depends not only on the quantity of money but fundamentally on its structure.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the diverging roles of cryptocurrency adoption in two distinct hybrid regimes: Iran and Türkiye, between 2020 and 2026. While both economies have faced severe financial instability, the drivers of crypto adoption differ fundamentally. By integrating on-chain data with macroeconomic indicators, this study demonstrates that while Turkish users primarily utilize stablecoins as a defensive retail hedge against persistent inflation and lira depreciation, Iranian users leverage digital assets as a strategic instrument for sanctions evasion and financial adaptation. Drawing on the 'weaponized interdependence' framework, we argue that cryptocurrency acts as a form of regulatory arbitrage that simultaneously mitigates and deepens financial fragmentation. Our findings provide empirical evidence of how digital assets reshape monetary sovereignty under external and domestic pressures.

title: The Labor-Market Impact of Board Gender Quotas and Disclosure Policies
affiliations: , Northeastern University and Harvard University - Business School (HBS)

detail.title: The Labor-Market Impact of Board Gender Quotas and Disclosure Policies
detail.abstract: Do board gender policies change women's labor-market outcomes beyond the boardroom? Using staggered policy introductions across European countries and synthetic control methods for staggered adoption, we estimate dynamic effects on board composition and employment and compare binding quotas with disclosure mandates. Board representation rises sharply, with the female share of board seats increasing by 6.63 percentage points in the announcement year and by 18.97 percentage points within five years. Quotas also raise the female share of full-time professional employment by 6.68 percentage points by year five, a roughly 13% relative gain from the pre-treatment baseline. Disclosure mandates produce similar initial effects but fade toward zero, consistent with weaker enforcement. We detect no effects on non-professional employment or on weekly hours worked. These results indicate that binding quotas generate gains in women's professional employment that extend well beyond the boardroom, while non-binding mandates do not.

detail.abstract: Properly managing healthcare data is a complex endeavor that must balance the requirements and interests of many stakeholders. In this paper, we present the findings from a panel discussion with healthcare professionals and academics, who elaborate on the current situation in healthcare data management as well as the future role that blockchain could play in this sector. Based on the findings of this panel, we structure the research field of healthcare data management and provide numerous avenues for future research. The outcome is a framework that highlights the important role of healthcare data and puts them into context. From a patient's perspective, we specifically elaborate on trust and privacy as well as the expected benefits. Additionally, four important data aspects are identified: integrity, security, interoperability, and, finally, sharing and transfer. We also outline the importance of current problems and derive several relevant and timely research questions that build the foundation of a research agenda for blockchain-driven innovation in healthcare data management. In summary, the framework will inform practitioners of blockchain's potential in healthcare and structure the area for researchers, who are called upon to investigate the respective topics in greater detail.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the growing role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in transforming consumer marketing through advanced personalization techniques in modern e-commerce. In an increasingly competitive digital marketplace, businesses are shifting from traditional segment-based marketing to individualized “segment-of-one” strategies powered by AI. The study explores how AI-driven personalization operates through data collection, predictive modeling, and real-time decision-making to deliver tailored customer experiences.

The paper highlights the key benefits of personalization, including enhanced customer engagement, improved brand loyalty, and increased conversion rates, while also emphasizing its impact on business efficiency and revenue generation. At the same time, it critically analyzes the challenges associated with AI implementation, particularly issues related to data privacy, algorithmic bias, and declining consumer trust.

Furthermore, the study discusses various personalization strategies such as behavioral targeting, collaborative filtering, context-aware marketing, and hyper-personalization using generative AI. It concludes that while AI-driven personalization offers significant competitive advantages, its long-term success depends on ethical practices, transparency, and responsible data management.

title: China, Commodities, and Chokepoints:  Market Signals in an Age of Geopolitical Disruption

detail.title: China, Commodities, and Chokepoints:  Market Signals in an Age of Geopolitical Disruption
detail.abstract: Absent supply shocks, China's dominance in global commodity markets has made the country's demand the single most important variable in industrial price formation worldwide. This brief article illustrates the role of Chinese demand in global commodity price formation, drawing on soybeans, crude oil, iron ore, and lithium carbonate as examples. China's demand influence, however, has been overshadowed by an acute geopolitical supply shock in the energy markets. Accordingly, the article examines the current disruption in global energy markets triggered by the Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which the International Energy Agency has called the largest oil supply disruption in history. The article concludes with practical guidance for institutional investors and chief investment officers, focusing on inflation-hedging, real-asset diversification, and risk monitoring in an environment of multi-year energy disruptions.

title: The Governance Gap Why Agentic AI Demands a New Project Execution Framework Version 1.0

detail.title: The Governance Gap Why Agentic AI Demands a New Project Execution Framework Version 1.0
detail.abstract: Every major software delivery methodology-Waterfall, Agile, SAFe-was designed to answer one question: did we build what we said we would build? That question assumes the software executes instructions. The moment software starts making autonomous decisions, the question changes entirely. This paper argues that the governance gap created by agentic AI is not a tooling problem, not a process problem, and not a maturity problem. It is a paradigm problem-and it requires a framework built from first principles around the governance of autonomous decisions, not the delivery of features. This paper introduces the Agentic Project Execution Framework (APEX): a governance-first delivery methodology that addresses the structural problems agentic AI introduces, replaces the Agile constructs that break down for autonomous systems, and provides organizations with a sequential, scalable model for building and governing agents at enterprise scale. APEX does not replace Agile for all software development. It replaces Agile specifically for software that decides-and provides the governance layer that Agile was never designed to deliver.

title: Hybrid New Venture Teams: How start-up teams consisting of full-time and part-time founders emerge, how they function and what makes them succeed
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of St. Gallen

detail.title: Hybrid New Venture Teams: How start-up teams consisting of full-time and part-time founders emerge, how they function and what makes them succeed
detail.abstract: Steve Wozniak (Apple) and Henry Ford (Ford) founded two of the most successful companies of all time while still being employed elsewhere. This combination of self-employment and salaried work, defined in the literature as hybrid or part-time entrepreneurship, represents more than half of the total startup activity worldwide. However, research in this field is still young and has mainly focused on individual entrepreneurs. In contrast, most startups today are founded by teams, so-called “New Venture Teams” (NVTs). This study examines how “Hybrid New Venture Teams” (HNVTs), consisting of both full- and part-time founders, emerge, function, and succeed. Using a comparative case study with 10 startup teams and 20 semi-structured interviews, it develops new theoretical insights into HNVTs. Findings show that HNVTs originate primarily from founders’ alternative commitments and personal circumstances. Team formation is constrained: part-time founders are accepted if they add resources and clarify when they will transition to full-time. A defining characteristic of HNVTs is the need to balance varying levels of risk-taking (commitment) and work effort (contribution). The transition to full-time, when all founders dedicate themselves fully to the venture, is a critical moment. Until then, the hybrid structure slows growth and creates potential for conflict. Therefore, HNVTs can be seen as transitional constructs, aiming to convert the startup into a full-time venture within one to two years. After this point, the HNVT becomes a typical NVT, according to existing entrepreneurship research. For long-term success, HNVTs must establish transparent communication, trust, and find effective compromises along their development process.

title: The Consumer Welfare Standard and the Protect Competition Standard: A Comparison and Assessment
affiliations: University of Utah - College of Social & Behavioral Sciences - Department of Economics, University of Utah - College of Social & Behavioral Sciences - Department of Economics and University of Houston Law Center

detail.title: The Consumer Welfare Standard and the Protect Competition Standard: A Comparison and Assessment

declarations.funderStatement: Institute for New Economic Thinking

publicationDetails.detailsText: Institute for New Economic Thinking Working Paper Series No. 248
publicationDetails.journalName: Institute for New Economic Thinking Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We compare the Consumer Welfare Standard (CWS) and the Protect Competition Standard (PCS) in antitrust. While the two standards are often viewed as mutually exclusive alternatives, there is a larger overlap between the two standards than is usually acknowledged. We first delineate each, recount their respective origins and identify the main supporters of each view. We then compare the two standards across several dimensions: we analyze the practical differences between the two standards in merger and monopolization cases; analyze their fidelity to Congressional intent and to Supreme Court precedent; and discuss how the two standards are connected to normative economic theory. Finally, we discuss the social welfare implications of the differing goals of the two standards. It is our hope that this piece may assist policy makers, courts, and antitrust practitioners better understand the two standards and how they can be more effectively and conscientiously applied.

title: Remorse Bias in Legal Decision-Making
affiliations: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey - School of Criminal Justice

detail.title: Remorse Bias in Legal Decision-Making
detail.abstract: Existing research suggests that a defendant's displays of remorse, frequently used to make attributions about their character, can act as valuable evidence for decision-makers in legal contexts. However, assessing remorse is a subjective process implicitly limited by human cognition, often stemming from expectations about how remorse should be expressed and whether some individuals are even capable of feeling it. This can lead legal decision-makers to potentially misread and discount a defendant's true feelings of remorse as disingenuous. Recent empirical work suggests that this social cognitive phenomenon, known as remorse bias, can lead to adverse outcomes for some defendants in the legal system-especially for those with personal characteristics that are commonly socially stereotyped or quite different from decision-makers' backgrounds. This article provides an overview of the concept of and recent empirical literature surrounding remorse bias in the legal system, including its impacts on decision-making and potential implications.

title: Crimes Against Campbell-Shiller
affiliations: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) and Michigan State University - Eli Broad College of Business

detail.title: Crimes Against Campbell-Shiller

publicationDetails.detailsText: Fisher College of Business Working Paper No. 2026-03-009
publicationDetails.journalName: Ohio State University, Fisher College of Business Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: Charles A. Dice Center Working Paper No. 2026-09

detail.abstract: The Campbell and Shiller (1988) log-linear approximation is widely viewed as a model-free accounting identity that always holds: in sample, in expectation, and under arbitrary subjective beliefs. None of these claims is true. The formula is far from automatic even in realized data. Many companies do not pay dividends, making the calculation ill-defined. For dividend payers, the results are not always what they seem. The formula registers buybacks and new issuance as phantom cash-flow shocks. Taking expectations comes with its own complications. Researchers see the forward-looking version of Campbell-Shiller as a dynamic Gordon model, but this interpretation requires investors to consistently think in present-value terms and to know the cap rate with basis-point precision. Both are strong assumptions that do not always hold in the data. Finally, the formula generically fails under arbitrary subjective beliefs. The exceptions represent knife-edge cases where forecast errors obey a precise adding-up condition. Insisting that Campbell-Shiller always holds makes it harder to learn about the true pricing model in the many cases where it does not.

title: Reframing Member Onboarding in Credit Unions: A Strategic Capability for Organizational Culture and Value Creation

detail.title: Reframing Member Onboarding in Credit Unions: A Strategic Capability for Organizational Culture and Value Creation
detail.abstract: Member onboarding has evolved into a critical strategic capability within credit unions, directly influencing member engagement, retention, and long-term value creation. While credit unions have historically emphasized member acquisition, insufficient attention to onboarding has contributed to high levels of account dormancy and limited product utilization. This article examines onboarding through an integrated framework combining relationship marketing theory, the resource-based view (RBV), and organizational culture perspectives. It argues that onboarding represents a foundational mechanism through which executive leadership operationalizes organizational culture and drives sustainable competitive advantage. Drawing on empirical research and industry evidence, the study demonstrates that early-stage engagement significantly shapes long-term member behavior, trust development, and financial outcomes. Furthermore, the article explores the role of digital transformation and leadership alignment in enhancing onboarding effectiveness. The findings suggest that credit unions that implement uctured, personalized, and technology-enabled onboarding processes achieve higher member retention, increased product penetration, and stronger institutional resilience. The article concludes with strategic recommendations for credit union leaders to reposition onboarding as a core driver of organizational performance and cooperative value creation.
