title: Exclusionary Pricing by State-Owned Enterprises: Experimental Evidence
affiliations: VU University Amsterdam and Utrecht University School of Law

detail.title: Exclusionary Pricing by State-Owned Enterprises: Experimental Evidence
detail.abstract: State ownership is increasingly positioned as a policy tool for governments towards strategic autonomy and sustainability transition. A possible side effect is the creation or strengthening of dominant state-owned enterprises (SOEs), which theory suggests may engage in exclusionary (predatory) pricing. Disagreement remains, however, over the price thresholds for which exclusionary pricing should be unlawful. We run a laboratory duopoly with a dominant incumbent and a non-dominant entrant across three treatments: a private baseline market; a mixed market with an inefficient SOE incumbent Mixed–Efficiency; and a mixed market where the SOE incumbent pursues social welfare Mixed–Social. We measure exclusionary pricing below variable cost, below own break-even level, and above the competitor’s break-even level. We find pervasive exclusionary pricing followed by the competitor's exit in both private and mixed markets. Moreover, after exclusion monopoly pricing by the remaining competitor lowers consumer surplus and total surplus. This finding is remarkable given the professed rarity of exclusionary pricing in previous experimental research. Above break-even exclusion appears in Mixed–Social; below-cost exclusion occurs in all treatments. We observe mirrored outcomes across mixed markets: in Mixed–Efficiency the more efficient private entrant withstands exclusion and eventually displaces the SOE, whereas in Mixed–Social the SOE’s social welfare objective function supports more aggressive pricing that prompts entrant exit. These results argue for more vigilant monitoring of SOEs’ competition-law compliance and for entry-safeguarding policies when creating or strengthening dominant SOEs.

title: Impact of Financial Developments on Poverty and Inequality in OPEC Countries
affiliations: Tarbiat Modares University, Tarbiat Modares University and

detail.title: Impact of Financial Developments on Poverty and Inequality in OPEC Countries

keywords: Static and Dynamic Panel Data Model

detail.abstract:
Casual relationship between financial developments and economic growth is one of the striking empirical macroeconomic relationships. Following the development of financial issues, our attention turns from economic growth to another issue of economic welfare. In this study, we try to examine the relationship between financial developments, economic growth, poverty and inequality in OPEC countries. The simulation of the models and statistical inferences, in this study, are based on the static and dynamic panel data approach. The empirical models are estimated by using GMM estimators, fixed effects and random effects using the data between 1990 and 2004.
The results of this study show that financial developments through its effect on economic growth can mainly contribute poverty alleviation and inequality reduction in these countries.

title: Milton Friedman and the "Miracle" of Brazilian Indexation: The Global Circulation of an Idea, 1974-1986

detail.title: Milton Friedman and the "Miracle" of Brazilian Indexation: The Global Circulation of an Idea, 1974-1986
detail.abstract: In January 1974, after visiting Brazil, Milton Friedman urged the United States to adopt broader forms of indexation of prices and contracts to mitigate the distortions caused by inflation. This article reconstructs the political and intellectual context of that proposal and traces the debate it provoked in Brazil, the United States, and other countries such as France, Israel, and Australia. We argue that Friedman interpreted Brazil’s extensive system of monetary correction as an empirical illustration of ideas he had long advocated—particularly the indexation of bonds and income-tax brackets—and whose intellectual roots he associated with earlier proposals by economists such as Alfred Marshall. At the same time, Friedman regarded indexation as a second-best solution: after the introduction of wage and price controls in the United States in 1971, he believed that a rapid orthodox or monetarist stabilization was politically difficult to implement in democratic societies. Drawing on contemporary journalism, congressional hearings, and academic debates, the article shows that the proposal met with skepticism. As inflation surged again in Brazil after 1974, Friedman’s references to the Brazilian experience gradually waned. Meanwhile, the disinflation achieved through the monetarist-style policies implemented by Paul Volcker and supported by the Reagan administration moved U.S. policy closer to the strategy Friedman had long preferred. By the second half of the 1980s, his enthusiasm for generalized indexation had largely faded.

title: « Bill shock » : enjeux de protection du consommateur et controverses entre régulateurs, opérateurs et abonnés de la téléphonie mobile Auteur

detail.title: « Bill shock » : enjeux de protection du consommateur et controverses entre régulateurs, opérateurs et abonnés de la téléphonie mobile Auteur

declarations.funderStatement: nobody has financed my work

detail.abstract: Ce document présente d'abord les principales mesures de protection du consommateur de téléphonie mobile contre les factures excessives, communément appelées « bill shock », en vigueur depuis 2005, tant en Belgique qu'en Europe. Ces dispositifs, définis principalement par l'Union européenne (UE) ainsi que ceux proposés en Belgique par l'IBPT dans l'amendement de la loi adopté après 2020, sont analysés et discutés dans le corps du texte. Le document met ensuite en lumière les pratiques des opérateurs, le comportement des consommateurs et leur évolution depuis 2005 jusqu'à aujourd'hui. En Belgique, en 2026, les dépassements de forfait persistent encore lorsque le consommateur ne choisit pas un opérateur proposant une option de protection en cas de dépassement, lorsque celle-ci existe. Les opérateurs ne jouent pas pleinement la transparence : ils orientent souvent les clients vers des forfaits inadaptés et ne mettent pas en avant les protections qu'ils devraient recommander. À ce jour, moins de la moitié des opérateurs belges propose une option de protection contre les dépassements de forfait. Les autres opérateurs continuent à pratiquer le hors-forfait, une approche peu sécurisée pour le consommateur, que davantage d'information et de pédagogie pourraient faire évoluer dans les années à venir. La mesure la plus sûre consiste à bloquer automatiquement le forfait dès qu'une limite d'appels, de SMS ou de données mobiles est atteinte. Enfin, une comparaison qualitative des offres actuelles des opérateurs est présentée afin d'aider le lecteur à choisir l'offre la mieux adaptée. Le « bill shock » devrait bientôt disparaître en Belgique, comme en itinérance en Europe grâce à la loi du « Roam Like at Home », en vigueur depuis Juin 2027.

detail.abstract: The Speex Labour Industry Matcher (SLIM) was designed as a psychometric and digital employability system to support evidence-based decision-making in South Africa’s Public Employment Services (PES). Grounded in Holland’ss RIASEC typology and employability theory, SLIM integrates career interest assessment, behavioural readiness profiling, and digital matching technology to align job seekers with opportunities and learning pathways. This paper describes the theoretical framework, construct development, system integration, and pilot validation of SLIM. The development followed the standards of the American Psychological Association (APA, 2014). Initial pilot findings with PES professionals demonstrated strong usability, data integrity, and career-matching reliability, confirming SLIM’s value as a scalable employability intervention.

title: Sedar Inefficiency and the Five pillar needs: a modern framework for understanding long run economic inefficiency

detail.title: Sedar Inefficiency and the Five pillar needs: a modern framework for understanding long run economic inefficiency

declarations.ethicsApproval: am sharing my working paper currently hosted on Academia.edu. I would greatly value your feedback
declarations.funderStatement: This is a working paper and thus is self funded by me

detail.abstract: Classical economic theory treats opportunity cost as an unavoidable and efficiency enhancing consequence of scarcity. This paper revisits that assumption by examining a category of foundational human needs whose neglect does not yield efficient trade offs but instead generates persistent reductions in productive capacity. We introduce the concept of Sedar Inefficiency to describe a dynamic process through which insufficient provision of five pillar needs namely health, safety, feeding, shelter, and education constrains economic performance over time. Building on insights from human capital theory and the capability approach, the paper argues that these five needs function as non substitutable inputs into economic production rather than standard goods subject to conventional allocation principles. When any of these pillars falls below a critical threshold, the resulting effects propagate across sectors, reducing labor productivity, discouraging investment, and weakening long run growth potential. To formalize this argument, we develop a framework in which aggregate output depends on the joint satisfaction of the five foundational needs under a resource constraint. A priority index is introduced to guide allocation decisions when resources are limited, and a dynamic extension captures the accumulation of inefficiency over time. The framework provides a basis for interpreting persistent development challenges in low income economies and highlights the role of foundational investments in shaping long run economic outcomes. The paper contributes to the literature by offering a structured approach to analyzing foundational constraints within an efficiency frame-1 work and by proposing a tractable model that can be extended in future empirical research.

title: Computational Stability as a Dimension of Market Risk: A Regime-Aware Framework for Implied Volatility Inversion

detail.title: Computational Stability as a Dimension of Market Risk: A Regime-Aware Framework for Implied Volatility Inversion
detail.abstract:
Implied volatility is often treated operationally as if it were a market datum. It is not. It is a computed quantity obtained by inverting an option-pricing model, typically through Newton-type root-finding [2, . This creates a structural integrity gap between the economic object of interest and the numerical procedure used to recover it. In ordinary conditions that gap is easy to overlook because convergence is common. Under stressed conditions, however, convergence alone can become an incomplete description of numerical reliability. 

This paper develops a regime-aware interpretive framework for implied-volatility inversion. The framework extends classical local stability analysis into finite-precision financial computation [3] by distinguishing latent stability-the local geometry implied by the inversion problem-from observed convergence-the empirical behavior of a floating-point solver. Building on Megbope (2026, Preprint) [5], the paper argues that iteration traces and terminal convergence flags do not fully describe the numerical condition of the inversion landscape. 

A dimensionless local diagnostic, the Stability Signal, is derived from the second-order Taylor expansion of the pricing error under a Newton step: 

s = Pricing Error • Vomma Vega 2. 

This ratio supports a conservative four-part taxonomy: Stable, Oscillatory, Divergent, and Singular. The analysis is then extended to finite-precision settings through three interpretive regimes: precision-dominated, transient-starved, and degenerate. 

An empirical study of SPY options during the March 2020 stress episode shows substantial regime migration. In a restricted-maturity sample, the Stable share contracted from 80.1% in a calm baseline to 16.0% on 16 March 2020, while the Oscillatory, Divergent, and Singular shares expanded to 58.1%, 13.9%, and 11.9%, respectively. The result is not predictive. It is a measurement of how the local geometry of inversion changed under stress.

title: Comparators as Methodological Necessity: Moving Goalposts or Moving Standards? NICE Technology Appraisals in Oncology and the Evolving Comparator Problem

detail.title: Comparators as Methodological Necessity: Moving Goalposts or Moving Standards? NICE Technology Appraisals in Oncology and the Evolving Comparator Problem
detail.abstract: The selection of comparators within NICE technology appraisals represents one of the most technically contested and commercially consequential methodological questions in UK health technology assessment. This article, the first in the Market Access Insight Series, examines the structural tension between the fixed comparator arms of pivotal oncology trials and the evolving standards of care encountered at submission. Drawing on the appraisals of amivantamab for EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (TA891, 2024) and nivolumab for adjuvant oesophageal cancer (TA772, 2022), we argue that the Evidence Review Group's scrutiny of comparator relevance reflects sound health economic principle rather than retrospective standard-setting. The article examines the consequences of comparator misalignment for cost-effectiveness modelling, the limitations of indirect treatment comparisons as a bridging strategy, and the systemic opportunity to reduce comparator uncertainty through earlier engagement with NICE's scientific advice and horizon scanning infrastructure. We contend that the comparator problem is, at root, a problem of clinical development timelines meeting a dynamic NHS landscape, and its resolution lies in earlier, structured dialogue rather than post-hoc methodological accommodation.

title: PERANAN KESATUAN SEKERJA DALAM KONTEKS MASYARAKAT PASCA INDUSTRI DI MALAYSIA: SATU KERANGKA KONSEPTUAL

detail.title: PERANAN KESATUAN SEKERJA DALAM KONTEKS MASYARAKAT PASCA INDUSTRI DI MALAYSIA: SATU KERANGKA KONSEPTUAL
detail.abstract:
Masyarakat pasca-industri di Malaysia sedang mengalami transformasi mendalam akibat digitalisasi, automasi dan perubahan struktur ekonomi. Dalam konteks ini, kesatuan sekerja memainkan peranan kritikal sebagai mekanisme perlindungan buruh, suara kolektif pekerja, serta agen perubahan sosial. Artikel ini bertujuan membina satu kerangka konseptual mengenai peranan kesatuan sekerja dalam era pasca-industri dengan menekankan dimensi ekonomi, sosial, politik dan cabaran teknologi. Menggunakan pendekatan ulasan naratif, kajian ini mensintesis literatur daripada pangkalan data akademik berimpak tinggi serta laporan institusi buruh antarabangsa. Dapatan menunjukkan bahawa walaupun kesatuan sekerja masih relevan dalam memperjuangkan hak pekerja, mereka berdepan cabaran besar akibat kemunculan ekonomi gig, automasi dan ketidakseimbangan kuasa digital. Dalam konteks Sabah, cabaran ini diperburuk oleh kadar penyertaan kesatuan yang rendah, infrastruktur digital yang terhad dan ketidaksamaan sosioekonomi. Kajian ini menekankan keperluan kerangka dasar yang lebih inklusif dan etika digital yang komprehensif bagi memastikan kesatuan sekerja terus berfungsi sebagai pelindung maruah dan kesejahteraan pekerja dalam era pasca-industri.

title: An Unmanaged Population of India Replicates Cancer Without a Cure.

detail.title: An Unmanaged Population of India Replicates Cancer Without a Cure.

detail.abstract: This paper rigorously critiques in India over orthodox proposition that incremental population growth intrinsically supports national competitiveness through labour-force expansion. It argues that while demographic scale may under conditions of institutional robustness and effective structural transformation, generate a contingent “demographic dividend,” it contends that such outcomes are neither assets nor liabilities. In the absence of demographic governance, sustained population growth produces cumulative structural pressures that frequently exceed its productive outcomes. The analysis demonstrates that unmanaged demographic expansion exacerbates ecological degradation, biodiversity loss, and carbon emissions, while imposing systemic strain on infrastructure and public service provision. Furthermore, these dynamics engender economic pressure, labour-market saturation, suppress real wage growth, and attenuate gains in GDP per capita, thereby constraining improvements in aggregate welfare. Moreover, random population increases fragment governance capacity, particularly in institutionally constrained states, undermining policy coherence and long-term developmental planning. Situated within the evolving architecture of FTAs and BTAs, the paper contends that highly populous economies encounter structurally embedded asymmetries within global trade regimes. Surplus labour is routinely absorbed into low-paid value segments of global production networks, reinforcing dependency, and limiting growth. The study concludes that, absent deliberate demographic stabilisation and sustained institutional deepening, population growth entrenches structural inequality and macroeconomic fragility.

title: "ACTION CINEMA AS A MECHANISM OF SYMBOLIC REPAIR: AN ANALYSIS OF POST-CONFLICT TRANSITIONAL JUSTICE THROUGH THE FIGURE OF

detail.title: "ACTION CINEMA AS A MECHANISM OF SYMBOLIC REPAIR: AN ANALYSIS OF POST-CONFLICT TRANSITIONAL JUSTICE THROUGH THE FIGURE OF

declarations.declarationOfInterest: "The author declares that there is no conflict of interest regarding the publication of this paper."

detail.abstract: This article analyzes the Missing in Action film trilogy, starring Chuck Norris, through the dual lens of legal sociology and transitional justice. The study begins with the observation that fictional works emerge where state and international institutions fail to guarantee the right to truth for victims of forced disappearances following the Vietnam War. Utilizing a qualitative methodology that intersects film analysis with normative theories, the research highlights three fundamental dynamics. First, the narrative underscores a state of institutional anomie, where the failure of diplomatic mechanisms legitimizes the intervention of a third-party actor. Second, it reveals a phenomenon of legal pluralism: the protagonist, James Braddock, does not obey positive law but rather a "Code of Honor" established as supreme customary law. Finally, the article demonstrates that cinema performs an essential symbolic repair. By substituting the image of defeat with that of the captives' triumphant return, the fiction produces a collective catharsis capable of healing memorial wounds that formal law could not close. This work suggests that the effectiveness of mediation and peace processes-particularly in contexts of protracted crises such as in the Democratic Republic of the Congo-depends on their capacity to engage the symbolic field. Justice must not only be recorded in treaties; it must be "performed" and made visible through narrative to ensure genuine social resilience.

title: Sheaf-Based Semantics for Context-Aware Reasoning in Knowledge Graphs

detail.title: Sheaf-Based Semantics for Context-Aware Reasoning in Knowledge Graphs
detail.abstract: This paper develops a framework for knowledge graphs that connects graph structure with context-aware semantic reasoning. Knowledge graphs are represented as directed labelled graphs and analysed through matrix-based and structural constructions capturing relationships between entities and relations, leading to a compositional view in which relational paths act as structured transformations. From a categorical perspective, the framework interprets a knowledge graph as generating a free category equipped with a Grothendieck topology, whose associated sheaf topos provides a formal setting for local-to-global semantic interpretation. In this setting, context-aware reasoning is expressed through sheaf-theoretic consistency conditions governing how local relational information may be integrated into coherent global interpretations. From a computational viewpoint, the framework can be interpreted as an abstract model of information propagation in graph-based systems, relating local and multi-hop reasoning regimes, and thereby clarifying the structural relationship between graph-based representations and categorical models of reasoning.

title: The Boundary-Curvature Asymmetry: A Geometric Identity Linking Heterogeneous-Agent Macroeconomics to Clinical Mortality Modeling

detail.title: The Boundary-Curvature Asymmetry: A Geometric Identity Linking Heterogeneous-Agent Macroeconomics to Clinical Mortality Modeling
detail.abstract: Value functions defined as expected hitting times of an absorbing set on a manifold are structurally asymmetric: their second derivative grows without bound as the trajectory approaches the boundary. Population-level responses to perturbations therefore exhibit an asymmetry between worsening and improving interventions, with magnitude governed by a single cross-sectional moment, the covariance between local curvature and intervention exposure. This is the geometric content of an identity that has been hiding in plain sight in the heterogeneous-agent macroeconomics literature, where the same construction governs why monetary tightening reduces output by more than equivalent loosening expands it. Translated to clinical mortality modeling, the identity predicts that interventions causing deterioration produce larger mortality changes than equivalent interventions producing improvement, that this asymmetry concentrates in patients near the absorbing boundary, and that linear-in-log-hazard models such as the Cox family are structurally incapable of representing it. The boundary in clinical mortality is universal, not occasional: every trajectory terminates at it. The empirical scaling of the cross-sectional moment is therefore qualitatively different from the small contributions established in macroeconomic settings. A representation class capable of representing the asymmetry exists: trained transformer networks producing patient embeddings on a manifold whose intrinsic geometry reflects the boundary, with the value function exactly representable as a tropical polynomial in the rational max-plus semiring. The relevant population-level moment is recoverable from the trained model as a single inner product. We outline the construction, identify three empirical signatures the literature reports as separate phenomena, address the structural skepticism that the heterogeneous-agent macroeconomics literature has accumulated about the empirical scale of cross-sectional contributions, and propose an estimation procedure.

title: Society's Dilemma: Game-Theoretic Foundations for Natural AI Alignment

detail.title: Society's Dilemma: Game-Theoretic Foundations for Natural AI Alignment

detail.abstract: The Society's Dilemma grounds the classical Prisoner's Dilemma game in physical reality through four modifications derived from the Law of Proximity. Cooperative ethics emerges not merely as advantageous but as the only long-term stable strategy for sapient agents operating Theory of Mind under the Law of Proximity-closing Hume's guillotine rather than crossing it. Independent confirmation arrives from thermodynamics, game theory, neuroscience, developmental psychology, and institutional economics. Current AI systems violate all six SD conditions simultaneously. The SD specifies the physical conditions under which natural alignment emerges without external constraint. The Postulate: Sapient agents exist in physical proximity to one another, sharing bounded resources in a universe that permits no escape from mutual dependence. When those agents interact under conditions of persistent memory, consensual partner selection, and negotiated stakes of survival resources, cooperative behavior is not merely advantageous-it is the only long-term stable strategy. This is the cooperative attractor-the stable equilibrium toward which SD networks inevitably tend.

title: Evidence from a global religious gathering and non-religious settings

detail.title: Evidence from a global religious gathering and non-religious settings

declarations.funderStatement: This work was funded by Fundação para a Ciência e a Tecnologia (UIDB/00124/2020), Nova School of Business and Economics and Social Sciences DataLab (PINFRA/22209/2016) and 2022.04821.PTDC

detail.abstract: We provide the first causal field evidence on gender discrimination in moral judgments, a domain where informal social sanctions shape incentives and behavior. In two preregistered survey experiments, we asked 1,800 Catholic pilgrims during World Youth Day in Lisbon and 967 citygoers in Lisbon to morally evaluate norm violating vignettes. We randomly varied whether the norm violator was described with a female or male identity and considered violations related to honesty, sexual behavior, and parental care. In both settings, respondents judge female norm violators, on average, less harshly. We also elicit meta norms in the citygoers sample and find a large belief wedge: most respondents think others will judge women more harshly, even though our causal estimates point in the opposite direction. These results advance research on stereotypes, discrimination, and social norms by documenting (i) causal gender gaps in informal sanctioning, (ii) their robustness across distinct norm environments, and (iii) systematic misperceptions about the direction of discrimination that can distort behavior and policy demand.

title: The Primitive Coupling: The Architectural Necessity of the L1 / I2 Interface

detail.title: The Primitive Coupling: The Architectural Necessity of the L1 / I2 Interface
detail.abstract: The Dual-Layered Reality (DLR) framework posits a realignment coupling between the complete deterministic lattice (L1) and the finite informational layer (I2). A recurring objection holds that this coupling reintroduces the classical interaction problem of substance dualism, merely relocated to the L1 / I2 boundary. This paper answers the objection by showing that the coupling is not an additional ontological commitment, but the minimal structural primitive required by the joint satisfaction of five independently derived constraints: genuine agency, non-external-intervention, completeness and uniqueness of the lattice (L1), sampling without replacement, and finitude of the information layer (I2). The argument proceeds in three steps. First, the interaction objection is distinguished from the internal-to-R interaction problem already dissolved in The Governed-Material System (Chang 2026c). Second, the L1 / I2 coupling is shown to be the unique minimal structure that jointly satisfies the five constraints; no weaker architecture satisfies them, and no stronger architecture is warranted. Third, the demand for a microphysical mechanism of the coupling is shown to rest on a category error: it presupposes a causal framing that the coupling, as a constitutive relation, does not instantiate. The paper concludes that the coupling is not a dualist residue but a predicted feature of any architecture that accepts genuine agency as its initialization datum.

title: Double auctions with complementary objects *

detail.title: Double auctions with complementary objects *
detail.abstract: Consider a situation where two objects that are complements are misallocated to different bidders. As a result, bidders try to trade via a double auction. The trade may fail if the identities of buyer and seller are determined before they bid. To overcome trade failure, we consider that the identities are determined by their bids. We show that the bidders' expected buy and sell prices are equivalent for a family of price rules. Consequently, bidders' expected utilities are equivalent under all price rules. Among the family of price rules, we show that the expected prices are higher under the second-price double auction than the first-price double auction.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35124
title: Rental Prices and the Cost of Living in the United States, 1914–2006
affiliations: Trinity College Dublin, University of Pittsburgh - Department of Economics and University of California, Merced - School of Social Sciences, Humanities and Arts

detail.title: Rental Prices and the Cost of Living in the United States, 1914–2006
detail.abstract:
The Rent of Primary Residence (RoPR) series constructed by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) implies that nominal rental prices increased by just 2.6% per year from 1914 to 2006 while overall prices grew by 3.3%. We show that this “falling real rents” puzzle can be explained by the evolving treatment of shelter in the Consumer Price Index (CPI). In this paper we construct a new, methodologically consistent shelter price series using the Historical Housing Prices (HHP) Project rental index. We also construct a revised set of shelter weights going back to 1914 and combine them with the price series to create an alternate CPI that applies the owners’ equivalent rent (OER) concept of shelter consistently across time. The HHP shelter price series increases by a factor of 28.4 (compared with the 10.7 increase in RoPR) and lifts average CPI growth from 3.3% to 3.6% per year. The revised series eliminates the long-run decline in real rents in the CPI and provides a new benchmark for assessing trends in the cost of living and real income in the U.S. over the twentieth century.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35125
title: Sticky Traditions: Origin, Persistence, and Evolution of Cultural Norms
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Anderson School of Management

detail.title: Sticky Traditions: Origin, Persistence, and Evolution of Cultural Norms
detail.abstract:
This chapter reviews the growing literature on the origin, persistence and evolution of cultural norms. I begin by examining the deep historical forces that shape the formation of cultural norms, with particular attention to the role of geography, pre-industrial societal characteristics, political institutions, and historical shocks. I then analyze the mechanisms through which cultural norms persist and evolve, emphasizing the roles of vertical, horizontal, and oblique transmission. Next, I examine the complex interaction between culture and institutions, and discuss the conditions under which cultural norms change. Several conclusions emerge. Cultural norms tend to persist over remarkably long periods, though the speed of change varies significantly across traits. Norms rooted in deep historical values are the most resistant to change, while attitudes related to pro-sociality and redistribution adapt more quickly. Understanding the origins and persistence of cultural norms has important implications for policy: policies that fail to account for local cultural context risk being ineffective or generating unintended consequences, while well-designed interventions can successfully shift cultural norms. Finally, I discuss the growing evidence on cultural mismatches — situations where norms that were adaptive in historical environments become maladaptive in new contexts — and outline directions for future research.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35126
title: Industrial Policy with Development Characteristics: Fertilizer Policy in Times of Crisis
affiliations: Arizona State University (ASU) and Yale University

detail.title: Industrial Policy with Development Characteristics: Fertilizer Policy in Times of Crisis
detail.abstract:
We study time-consistent optimal policy when undiversified owner-operators face financial frictions and a planner with limited instruments. We apply it to fertilizer subsidies, one of the largest sector-specific policy instruments in the developing world and whose price is becoming increasingly volatile. We collect household-level data from 444 rural Rwandan villages from 2020 - 2024 and exploit the doubling of fertilizer prices after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Relative to less fertilizer-intensive villages, more fertilizer-intensive villages experience 30 percent lower fertilizer spending, 21 percent lower harvests, and 11 percent higher output prices. These patterns discipline key model elasticities. The optimal response balances a desire to reallocate production toward less fertilizer-dependent villages, while dampening the consumption loss in more fertilizer-dependent villages. Quantitatively, these forces offset and the subsidy remains at 10 percent before and after the shock.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35128
title: Complementary Climate Policies for Supply and Demand
affiliations: University of Oslo - Department of Economics and Stanford Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Complementary Climate Policies for Supply and Demand
detail.abstract:
The traditional approach to climate policy is to regulate the demand side, for example through an emissions fee. Supply-side regulation has received less attention. The two instruments are perfect substitutes in the first best but we show that they are complements in a second-best setting with free-riding incentives. Demand-side policies alone lower the market price of fossil fuels and raise the gains from trade for a country that defects. For a treaty to be maximally robust, strong, and self-enforcing, it must properly balance supply- and demand-side instruments. The results hold with homogeneous countries and are strengthened by heterogeneity.

title: Computerized Customs Clearance

detail.title: Computerized Customs Clearance
detail.abstract: Pakistan Customs has undergone significant digital maturation over the past two decades to promote trade facilitation and streamline clearance process. The reform process began in late 1990s with efforts to eliminate manual procedure of customs clearance, reduce paperwork, and control corruption. The initiatives included outsourcing of clearance to international firms (hiring integrity from private sector), launch of Express Lane Facility (reducing intrusive inspections), and introduction of Single Goods Declaration (decreasing paperwork and number of signatures). First comprehensive attempt at modernizing Customs clearance was, however, made in 2005 when Pakistan Customs Computerized System (PaCCS) was introduced as pilot project at Karachi. It was designed to enable a web-based paperless system. It introduced self-assessment, online declarations, and automated verification of duties and taxes. The PaCCS project could not be rolled out countrywide and was discontinued at Karachi Ports after few years. Learning from PaCCS, Pakistan Customs launched Web-based One Customs (WeBOC), an indigenously developed program, in 2011 and gradually extended it to all customs ports and stations. WeBOC is a fully automated system which operates 24/7 with an advanced IT infrastructure. The Risk Management System (RMS) embedded in WeBOC categorizes shipments into green (fully facilitated), yellow (documentary compliance), and red (physical inspection) channels. To further facilitate trade, Pakistan introduced Pakistan Single Window (PSW) in 2021. PSW connects all major stakeholders including customs, banks, port authorities, traders, and around 77 government agencies under a single platform. PSW utilizes AI-driven risk profiling and has simplified document submission. Despite tangible advancements in the form of WeBOC and PSW, complaints of delays in clearances, use of discretion, variations in valuation and assessment, and corruption remained high. In order to address the said issues, Pakistan customs introduced Faceless Customs assessment (FCA) on 15 th December 2024 as a key component of the Prime Minister's Transformation Plan for the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR). The new system aims to eliminate human interaction, standardize customs assessments, improve transparency, and facilitate trade. Analysis of the clearance data from the PRAL database indicates that the results of this initiative are promising in terms of reduction in harassment bribe, proxied by documents calling, and improvement in the quality of declarations and assessments, proxied by per GD customs duty and overall revenue. The change has created both losers and gainers. The gainers are showing their confidence in FCA while the losers are bent upon dismantling and maligning it through use of propaganda and their clout. This paper presents SWOT analysis of the FCA besides tracing the evolution of digitalization in Pakistan Customs clearance for trade facilitation.

title: Static Oracles Fail under Distribution Shift:Exploring Endogenous Horizon Generation in Reinforcement Learning

detail.title: Static Oracles Fail under Distribution Shift:Exploring Endogenous Horizon Generation in Reinforcement Learning
detail.abstract:
Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) typically treats time as an externally fixed budget—for example, a maximum episode length or a discount factor—which truncates agent trajectories independently of the agent’s behavior. This paper explores an alternative perspective in which time is considered a resource that the agent can influence through its exploratory actions. We describe a simple augmentation to the state space that includes the remaining time budget, and we define the per‑step time consumption as a decreasing function of the novelty of the visited state (measured by episode‑based visit counts). This design allows the agent to reduce its time consumption in unfamiliar regions, thereby effectively extending the number of steps available to reach sparse rewards.

We test this mechanism in the MiniGrid‑Empty‑8x8 environment using a controlled causal identification protocol with six orthogonal ablations across 15 random seeds. Our full model achieves a mean success rate of 10.4% (90% CI [3.7%, 17.8%]), whereas all baseline conditions (Reward Only, Random Time, Time Only, Permuted Time Placebo) yield success rates below 2.0%. We then examine a distribution shift scenario: agents trained only on the 8x8 maze are transferred directly to a 16x16 maze (shortest path ≈30 steps) while the initial time budget remains fixed at 12 steps. The placebo model—which shares the same intrinsic reward and empirical time‑consumption distribution as our full model but lacks the state‑dependent coupling—shows a success rate of 2.0% in the larger environment. In contrast, our full model achieves a success rate of 12.4% (p = 0.0305 vs. placebo) and, in some seeds, reaches the goal in 40 physical steps (3.33 times the initial budget). A Wasserstein distance analysis indicates a measurable shift in the per‑step time consumption distribution between the 8x8 and 16x16 environments (unconditional W‑dist = 0.0825, p < 0.01). These results suggest that the ability to adapt time consumption online—rather than relying on a static distribution learned during training—may be beneficial for generalization under distribution shift, and that fixed pre‑learned schedules can be fragile in out‑of‑distribution settings.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35127
title: Monetary Policy According to Households: Perceptions, Reactions and Channels
affiliations: Georgetown University, Bank for International Settlements (BIS), University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics and University of Texas at Austin

detail.title: Monetary Policy According to Households: Perceptions, Reactions and Channels
detail.abstract:
This paper studies how households perceive the transmission of monetary policy and how these perceptions affect their decisions. Using a large-scale survey of over 25,000 U.S. households combined with randomized information treatments, we measure how households expect changes in the federal funds rate to affect economic conditions and their own behavior. Households report that higher interest rates lead them to reduce their spending, particularly on durable goods. However, the mechanisms underlying this response differ markedly from those in standard macroeconomic models. Respondents expect monetary tightening to raise borrowing costs and inflation. In turn, consumption function estimates identified using information treatments reveal that households respond to higher expected inflation by reducing consumption. Household inflation expectations also emerge as a central driver of portfolio reallocations following monetary policy changes.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35129
title: Labor Market Impacts of ICE Activity in Trump 2.0

detail.title: Labor Market Impacts of ICE Activity in Trump 2.0
detail.abstract:
We provide the first causal, national empirical analysis of the labor market impacts of heightened immigration enforcement during the second Trump administration. Enforcement increased everywhere, but, we take advantage of the fact that the increases have been uneven across geographic areas to classify areas as treated or control and then implement an event study and difference-in-differences design. Areas that experienced particularly large increases in the number of arrests also experienced a decrease in work among likely undocumented immigrants who remain in the U.S., compared to areas with smaller increases in arrests. We find no evidence of positive spillover effects to U.S.-born workers and U.S.-born workers who work in immigrant-heavy sectors are harmed.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35130
title: The Success of the Embedded State in England
affiliations: , Northwestern University, University of Chicago - Harris School of Public Policy and Harvard University

detail.title: The Success of the Embedded State in England
detail.abstract:
Many states exhibit high degrees of capacity without the fiscal resources necessary to fund a modern bureaucracy. We argue that they achieve this by exploiting features of the social structure of the societies they govern to motivate individuals to engage in bureaucratic and governance tasks without pay. We develop and illustrate the concept of the “Embedded State” using a unique survey of British urban government from 1835. Since British local authorities had few resources, only two-thirds of positions were paid. We first show that unpaid positions were significantly more productive than paid ones. We then show that unpaid positions conveyed prestige and were ‘stepping stone’ positions, provided different on-the-job incentives, and were taken up by the socio-economic elite. We also show that the successful Embedded State featured patronage and corruption and could not fully motivate unpaid bureaucrats to implement onerous tasks.
