detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the role of actively managed fixed income in defined contribution plans by translating reasonable excess returns into economically meaningful retirement outcomes using a 227‑year dataset of historical returns and inflation in the U.S. Relative to passive‑only investments, the additional returns from active fixed income are estimated to substantially improve retirement sustainability—extending asset longevity, enabling earlier retirement, reducing required savings and employer contributions while working, or supporting higher sustainable real spending. For a typical 20‑year retirement, these effects include 25% longer retirement horizons, retirement several years earlier, a 30%+ increase in match rates, or sustainable spending increases of roughly 9%, with benefits growing at longer horizons. Extending the analysis to include private credit, we find comparable impacts of private assets, and that combining both active public and private fixed income further amplifies these gains, yielding improvements that are large, robust across historical regimes.

detail.title: Asymptotic-Guided Deep BSDEs for Non-Semimartingale Optimal Control: Addressing the Curse of Dimensionality in Rough Volatility Models

detail.abstract: Optimal execution under rough volatility loses the Markov property, creating complex stochastic control problems. While the Markovian lift restores Markovianity by expanding the state space, the resulting high-dimensional Backward Stochastic Differential Equations (BSDEs) are notoriously difficult to solve due to the quadratic Hamiltonian, which frequently leads to gradient stagnation in standard deep learning methods. To address this, we propose the Asymptotic-Guided Deep BSDE framework. By leveraging an analytical prior derived from singular perturbation theory to resolve the macroscopic inventory trajectory, we analytically shrink the learning target from O(1) to O(ϵ). This transforms the high-dimensional BSDE into a small-noise residual learning problem, effectively flattening the optimization landscape and mitigating the gradient stagnation typical of black-box solvers. We validate our framework against exact finite difference benchmarks in low dimensions. Furthermore, in scalability tests up to a 52-dimensional state space (N = 50 rough volatility factors), our hybrid method maintains stable convergence and significantly mitigates the curse of dimensionality, achieving an approximately 67% reduction in error and 18% faster convergence compared to standard Deep BSDEs that exhibit severe stagnation and instability.

title: Roles: Nomos Paradigm Series · Article 2a — An analytical series based on Physis: A Theory of Power (Öztürk, 2026)

detail.abstract: This article is the second piece of the Nomos Paradigm Series, applying the framework of Physis: A Theory of Power (Öztürk, 2026) to the structural history of the upper-class roles that have governed human civilization. The article advances four interlocking claims. First, the roles capable of constituting the upper class are structurally limited in number — not by historical accident but because hegemony-generating capacity itself derives from a finite set of capability-families (force, meaning, capital, institutional operation), and the dominant roles are those producing the purest forms of power within these families. Second, throughout the aristocratic paradigm three principal roles — aristocrat, clergy, warrior — carried the upper-class struggle for thousands of years across virtually all geographies, while the merchant role, despite recurrent emergence, was structurally suppressed wherever the paradigm permitted no opening. Third, the rise of the merchant role to the upper class is the sole radical role-transformation in five thousand years of human history; it became possible only through a specific structural conjuncture in European geography — intra-paradigm competition, scale, and openness of field — and proceeded through three historical moments (Magna Carta 1215, the shaping of Parliament, the English Civil War 1649) that progressively unbound the politician role from its origin as an aristocratic bargaining instrument. Fourth, the bourgeois paradigm has matured into a structural condition in which corporate entities govern corporate entities, with the V3–V4 orientation (Article 1) emerging as a structural pressure rather than a technological choice — the temporal asymmetry of bureaucracy, the dissolution of the lower class's source-hegemony, and the upper class's need to apply the flow of will without dilution converging into a singular trajectory. The framework specifies its own falsification conditions: if a fifth family of hegemony-generating capacity is demonstrated, or if the structural asymmetry of the bourgeois paradigm is resolved by full mutual swallowing, the central theses collapse.

title: Externalities and the Matching Principle: The Case for Reallocating Environmental Regulatory Authority
affiliations: George Mason University - Antonin Scalia Law School and Yale Law School

detail.title: Externalities and the Matching Principle: The Case for Reallocating Environmental Regulatory Authority

publicationDetails.detailsText: Yale Law & Policy Review, Vol. 14, pp. 23–66 (1996)

detail.abstract:
The extreme centralization of environmental regulation is the result of interest group politics and dramatic political developments rather than a sober analysis of the major trade-offs involved in moving to federal domination of environmental protection. During the late 1960s and early 1970s, many environmental concerns that had previously been thought of as purely local issues, such as solid waste disposal, became federal issues. Although there is little doubt that national politicians were ahead of the curve in terms of responding to environmental concerns, one must not then assume that state and local politicians would have continued to be unresponsive to environmental issues arising in their own backyards. Nevertheless, there appears to be a oneway ratchet in the federal system—once a federal issue, always a federal issue. Moreover, among many environmentalists, there remains a deep distrust of state and local control of environmental quality. An analysis of the incentives of state and local politicians suggests that this distrust may not be justified.

This study considers whether environmental policy can be improved by reallocating authority for environmental regulation within our federal system. Our primary focus is on the institutional setting in which environmental policies are adopted. A fundamental issue is how to allocate regulatory authority so that political institutions and processes will yield policies that achieve the optimal or efficient level of pollution without imposing unnecessary costs on productive economic activity. Because there is no known answer to the critical question, “What is the optimal level of pollution?,” policy analysts often assert that the determination of the tolerated amount of pollution is a political question. Although “invocations of the superiority of political processes for resolving issues of social and economic policy” are commonplace, the assertion that a policy issue is a political problem does not solve the policy issue because alternative political institutions are likely to yield different answers.

Alternative political policymaking institutions, such as state and national legislatures, can be analyzed to determine which institutions are best suited to weighing costs and benefits in the determination of the optimal level of pollution. To the extent that all relevant costs and benefits are taken into account in the political decision-making process, “better” policies should emerge. In this regard, we develop the Matching Principle as a guide to determining the most efficient governmental level for regulation of different types of environmental concerns. The Matching Principle suggests that, in general, the size of the geographic area affected by a specific pollution source should determine the appropriate governmental level for responding to the pollution. There is no need for the regulating jurisdiction to be larger than the regulated activity. In other words, when a particular polluting activity is limited to a particular locality or state, there is very little justification for federal environmental regulation. When a federal government response is justified, it should be the most limited response possible.

Although the Matching Principle may seem radical to some environmentalists, this idea has a long history in American constitutional law and theory. As James Wilson explained at the Pennsylvania ratifying convention, “Whatever object of government is confined in its operation and effect, within the bounds of a particular State, should be considered as belonging to the government of that State.” As Professor McConnell has observed, Wilson’s view, which was the dominant perspective in the debates of the period, “stands in marked contrast to the modem tendency to resolve all doubts in favor of federal control.” And, as we will show, many important environmental problems are problems of purely local concern, and should be regulated at the local level. In particular, many of the sites targeted by Superfund are contained within the confines of a single state. The cleanup of these sites presents issues of purely local concern, and the economic theory of federalism articulated in this paper, which is entirely consistent with the Framers’ design, would confine authority over these issues to local regulators. Under our Matching Principle, if the federal government wants to intrude on local decision-making authority over the cleanup of local sites, it should confine itself to lending expertise and providing funding. It should refrain from imposing substantive standards or imposing legal liability.

title: Honesty as a “communicative tool” in sentencing: A study of judges in the U.S. and Australia
affiliations: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey - School of Criminal Justice, Flinders University, Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey - School of Criminal Justice and Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey - School of Criminal Justice

detail.title: Honesty as a “communicative tool” in sentencing: A study of judges in the U.S. and Australia
detail.abstract: This study, drawing from interviews with trial court judges in the U.S. and Australia (N = 47), builds a theoretical qualitative model that illustrates the conceptualization, significance, and influence of a defendant's honesty as a “communicative tool” in punishment and sentencing practices for judges in these jurisdictions. A constant comparative analysis shows that judges from both jurisdictions generally believe that a defendant's honesty acts as a communicative tool during sentencing, and this can lead them to reconfigure their sentencing practices–which they view as representing the interests of victims and the community–to prioritize mercy as well as rehabilitative and reparative ideals. Further, judges look for defendants to communicate honesty in ways that enable them to develop a complete understanding of its weight during sentencing, with U.S. judges particularly focusing on body language and nonverbal indicators. Overall, this study not only represents the first known empirical examination of a defendant's honesty within the communicative theory of punishment framework but also assesses if and how it translates across national cultures and criminal-legal systems, as well as how judges believe guidelines and legislation limit sentencing decisions involving honesty in Australia and the U.S. Implications of this work for sentencing practices are discussed.

detail.abstract: Many startups in the 2000s have remained private after achieving large valuations, a pattern that funding availability alone cannot explain. We propose that startups relying heavily on organization capital to achieve economies of scale and network effects through digital technologies are more likely to become large private firms than exit earlier via an IPO or acquisition. Using LinkedIn data, we construct a novel measure of organization capital intensity for startups. Exploiting a legal shock that strengthened organization capital protection, we provide causal evidence that organization-capital-intensive startups are more likely to remain private and grow large rather than exit early.

detail.abstract: This paper revisits the Gilchrist and Zakrajšek (2012) predictive regression models for payroll employment, unemployment, and industrial production. The models only predicted well in-sample. They did not predict well out-of-sample. They only ever predicted well during stagflation and during and in the immediate aftermath of the Global Financial Crisis. The models hinted at successful out-of-sample performance only for unemployment. An improved version should include real stock market return and the Baa spread and be winsorized for its most extreme forecasts. title: Racially Disparate Effects of the Japan Trade Shock: The Role of Occupational Exposure
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Racially Disparate Effects of the Japan Trade Shock: The Role of Occupational Exposure
detail.abstract: We study how the Japan trade shock generated racially disparate labor market outcomes. Using detailed establishment-level data and a shift-share IV design, we show that the Japanese trade exposure decreased Black and White manufacturing employment, with substantially larger effects on Black workers. Two-thirds of the decrease in Black operator employment (relative to that of White operators) was due to disparate occupational exposure. Disparate exposure was associated with local anti-Black prejudice. The Japan shock decreased Black incomes and persistently increased Black poverty. These results show that aggregate sector-level trade shocks can hit minority workers particularly hard when they are concentrated in exposed occupations.

title: Is Informed Short Selling Concentrated in Family Firms? Evidence from a Reinvestigation
affiliations: University of Illinois at Chicago - College of Business Administration, University of Louisville - Department of Finance and University of Kansas - Finance Area

detail.title: Is Informed Short Selling Concentrated in Family Firms? Evidence from a Reinvestigation
detail.abstract: We reinvestigate Anderson, Reeb, and Zhao's (2012) findings that informed short selling is unique to family firms and driven by information leakage from internal disputes. Using the same firm sample and more comprehensive short-selling data, we find that short selling predicts future returns in both family and nonfamily firms. We also find no significant difference in abnormal short selling before negative earnings announcements. In extended sample periods, short selling continues to predict returns for nonfamily firms under both ownership-based and familial-link definitions. Overall, our evidence suggests that short sellers are broadly informed and that family firms are not uniquely vulnerable.

title: Objectivity as Stable Path Availability Structure - Subjectivity, Intersubjectivity, Perceived Freedom, and Operative Freedom in the Architecture of Freedom Intelligence

detail.title: Objectivity as Stable Path Availability Structure - Subjectivity, Intersubjectivity, Perceived Freedom, and Operative Freedom in the Architecture of Freedom Intelligence
detail.abstract: I propose a scientific reconstruction of the concepts of objectivity, subjectivity, intersubjectivity, perceived freedom, and operative freedom inside the Architecture of Freedom Intelligence. The thesis is that objectivity is not perceptionless truth but stable path structure across trained perceptions, observers, instruments, contexts, and methods. Subjectivity is not error but situated path access. Intersubjectivity is not consensus but coordinated path differentiation across observers. The argument rests on a single empirical asymmetry: structural distortion of paths is approximately observer-independent, while perception of paths is observer-dependent. The same staircase imposes the same geometry on every body that approaches it but produces different operative freedoms for different bodies and instruments. From this asymmetry I derive five layers-Absolute Freedom, objective path structure, shared perceived freedom, individual perceived freedom, and operative freedom-and show that they are not interchangeable. Freedom is infinite in absolute terms; operative freedom is situated. The Law of Freedom does not measure freedom itself; it measures access to real paths under structural distortion and recursive observer-structure state. The paper proceeds by operational definitions, examples, counterfactual stress tests, and methodological prescriptions. Each conceptual move is paired with a falsification test.

title: There Is No Pathlessness

detail.title: There Is No Pathlessness
detail.abstract: I propose that freedom is the true cause of reality because freedom means path availability, and there is no possibility of pathlessness. Everything that exists navigates: water down a slope, photons through a slit, ions across a membrane, a child across a room, a household across a budget. Intelligence is the capacity, in any system, to perceive the lightest available path within a given context and to reduce distortion so that path can become real. I call this the Architecture of Freedom Intelligence (AFI). This paper investigates the hypothesis as a structural claim, not a sentimental one. I review the principal historical statements on freedom, change, possibility, will, action, and affordance from Heraclitus to Norman; I identify nine load-bearing gaps that no existing framework closes simultaneously; I formalise the AFI five-thesis architecture with its operational law, its dynamic law, and its law of motion; and I demonstrate the framework's usefulness by deriving design implications for housing, kindergartens, tools, AI, and the spatial economy. The paper does not claim that AFI replaces physics. It claims that physics is metafreedom — the measurable grammar of freedom under constraint — and that a useful theory of everything must include not only forces and fields but the navigation of lived space. The central operative claim, written in words throughout this paper, is that the freedom of a structure equals the perception of available paths divided by the distortion of available paths, raised to alpha-infinite recursion.

title: TurboTax Terror: How Lobbyists Made Tax-Time Terrible, and How Congress Can Fix It
affiliations: University of Washington - School of Law, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Washington

detail.title: TurboTax Terror: How Lobbyists Made Tax-Time Terrible, and How Congress Can Fix It
detail.abstract: In most first-world nations, the government simply sends citizens their tax return annually, because it already knows how much money people make. Then, taxpayers adjust their bill on the margins to account for their own personal situation. Conversely, the U.S. requires that each individual must completely prepare their tax return on their own. We have a notoriously complicated tax code, which makes the need to pay for professional help and tax preparation software practically a necessity. That has led to booming business for tax preparation companies like Intuit, the maker of TurboTax, which markets itself as an efficient, consumer-friendly choice to handle tax-time each April.

title: Improving the Realism of Multi-Agent Simulation Models for Airport Surface Movement Operations: Trajectory-based Calibration, Towing Operations, and Operational Variations
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Independent

detail.title: Improving the Realism of Multi-Agent Simulation Models for Airport Surface Movement Operations: Trajectory-based Calibration, Towing Operations, and Operational Variations

declarations.funderStatement: This research has received funding as part of the ASTAIR - Auto Steer Taxi at AIRport project from SESAR 3 JU under Grant Agreement No. 101114684 under European Union’s Horizon Europe research and innovation programme.

detail.abstract: Airside operations at major airports are becoming increasingly complex due to growing traffic demand, environmental constraints, new technologies, and infrastructure limitations. To support operational improvements and evaluate existing and future concepts of operations, both research and industry increasingly rely on fast-time models and digital twins of airport operations. Yet, the value of these tools depends critically on their ability to represent operational behaviour with sufficient fidelity. Agent-based models are well suited to this task, as they can capture heterogeneous actors, local interactions, and emergent system-level effects. In this paper, we calibrate and extend a computational multiagent system (MAS) model for studying next-generation airport surface movement operations at major airports. Using Amsterdam Airport Schiphol as a case study, three aspects of model realism and operational relevance are addressed. First, historical ground trajectories are projected onto a detailed graph of the taxiway network to derive realistic aircraft dynamics and refined A-CDM milestones. The calibrated model shows close agreement with observed taxi times, taxi distances, and infrastructure occupancy rates. Second, aircraft towing operations are incorporated to assess their system-level effects. The simulations show that additional towing can substantially increase connected stand capacity. Moreover, under a centralised coordination scheme, even high towing volumes do not adversely affect taxiing performance. Third, operational variations are analysed to evaluate the effects of reduced takeoff separations and more progressive taxi speed limits, both of which improve operational performance by around 10%. Across the analyses, departure runways emerge as the dominant bottleneck at Schiphol, while realistic speed profiles and selective towing offer operationally relevant efficiency gains. Overall, the results demonstrate how combining trajectory-based calibration with MAS modelling can provide actionable insights for improving the efficiency and predictability of airport airside operations.

title: European Statistics Begin to Sing: Missing Juniors, and Why Demographics Won't Explain It

detail.title: European Statistics Begin to Sing: Missing Juniors, and Why Demographics Won't Explain It
detail.abstract: In the last three years, generative AI was everywhere in firms' narratives but barely visible in official labour statistics. In Europe, this may be changing. Combining EU Labour Force Survey data with the Eurostat enterprise survey on AI adoption, it is now possible to identify some first crosscountry EU evidence, drawn from harmonised official statistics, of post-GenAI movements in the labour force linked to the actual adoption of, and not merely exposure to, generative AI. One of the strongest patterns emerging from the statistics confirms the so-called seniority bias: the data show a clear post-2022 divergence in the age composition of High-AI sectors. In the NACE sectors with the highest AI adoption rates, the youngest workers lose relative ground while senior workers continue to gain, a divergence that does not appear in the economy as a whole, let alone in low-adoption sectors. The pattern cannot be reduced to demographic ageing, as it is not driven by a contraction of the young population at large.

title: Training Perception for the Lightest Paths - Why Intelligence Requires Going Against Lazy Perception

detail.title: Training Perception for the Lightest Paths - Why Intelligence Requires Going Against Lazy Perception
detail.abstract: I argue, in the framework of the Architecture of Freedom Intelligence, that the central problem of intelligence is not choice but perception, because every system follows the lightest path it can perceive and the lightest visible path is, in distorted regimes, often a heavy real path in disguise. Perception, untrained, is structurally lazy: it accepts the most immediately visible, socially inherited, emotionally relieving, or low-effort alternative as if it were the lightest real path. Intelligence, on the framework's narrow definition, is the trained capacity to perceive the lightest real path inside a context of distortion. The paper develops the AFI account of perception across four operational levels-passive physics, topological, agent-aligned, structural pre-execution-and articulates the training disciplines that widen perception across substrates. It distinguishes apparent lightness from real lightness, abstract why-statements from structural ones, and study from the perception-training that good study can but does not necessarily perform. It positions meditation as direct work on internal distortion, design as perception training for inhabitants, and good teaching as master guidance rather than transmission. It applies the framework to life decisions, housing, planta smart homes, AI, tools, education, and society, and it closes with the open frontiers-the Logic-layer perception gap, the structural account of perceptual transfer, and the operationalisation of perception-training AI.

title: Introducing Perception in Navigation Systems

detail.title: Introducing Perception in Navigation Systems
detail.abstract: I introduce perception as the missing operative variable between freedom, distortion, physics, design, and intelligence. In the Architecture of Freedom Intelligence (AFI), freedom is path availability, distortion is path deformation, and intelligence is contextual lightest-path perception that liquifies distortion. Perception, in this paper, is defined strictly Perception in Navigation Systems • AFI agent-relative differentiation function that turns objective availability into operative freedom. Without that variable, no theory of physics can reach knowledge, intelligence, or design, because all three are species of perception against a structured world. Perception is the bridge a Theory of Everything has been missing.
